['One of the last remarks made by the hon. member for Hochelaga (Mr. Rivet), who has just taken his seat, was to the effect that he had carefully read the motion which is before the House. Of all the remarks uttered by that gentleman that was the most surprising to me, because, throughout the entire course of an address lasting I believe over an hour, it was the only remark that bore any possible relation to the words of the motion at all. I regret that, owing to the lateness of the hour, and owing to the fact that to answer the hon. gentleman would require me to disregard utterly the motion itself, it will be impossible for me to give much attention to his address. As to the gentleman who preceded him, the hon. member for Berthier (Mr. Ee-rement), who spoke in French, I regret, with my hon. friend from NoTth Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) that I was unable to understand his address. I regret it all the more because, though not able to understand it, I was able to appreciate the music of his voice and accent, and the apparent eloquence of his language.
The Minister of Marine and Fisheries has exhibited some remarkable qualities during the present session. I must congratulate him on the marvellous facility of intellect and the bewildering dexterity of mind that enable him to come to almost any conclusion that may be congenital to him, or satisfactory to his conscience, utterly irrespective of the facts. On April 30, almost a year ago, when his department, in conjunction with other departments, stood charged before the country with the most serious delinquencies, when he himself, as part of the department, stood charged with a lack of conscience, when his department stood charged with being utterly wanting in a directing head, as far as the commissioners could see, the minister saw fit to come before the House and tell of the hard work he had done in his department, to recount the undertakings he had carried out in the St. Lawrence river, and up in the neighbourhood of Port Arthur. No doubt he conceived that that was an answer to the charge of the Royal Commission. And when the hon. member for St. Anne (Mr. Doherty) saw fit to state that the resolution as it stands does not call in question, and does not make a question in this debate,', "of the character and integrity of the minister himself, the minister saw fit at once to come to the conclusion that the member for St. Anne, speaking for this side of the House, had acknowledged the integrity of the character of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries as head of that department. Surely that was a delightful contortion of the mind, that was a beautiful piece of reasoning. The Minister of Marine has also come to another conclusion very satisfactory to his conscience. He comes before this parliament, and before we were in session more than a week, he assured this House that he had received a certificate of character, not only from the hon. member for St. Anne, but front this commission. He assured this House, and it is now on record, that he came out with his skirts clear from the report of Mr. Justice Cassels. Now it is indeed a beautiful piece of reasoning for the minister to come to the conclusion that his skirts are clear by an investigation through a commission which was forbidden above all things to investigate anything about him at all. The hon. member for Richmond also says that it can no longer be said that there is any charge against the minister, or any suspicion that can be levelled against him, because, he says, the minister is cleared by the report of Mr. Justice Cassels. But the hon. member for Richmond made that statement in face of the assurance of the Minister of Agriculture, in face of the assurance of the Attorney General of this country, in face of the assurance of the Minister of Marine himself, and of the Prime Minister himself, that Mr. Justice Cassels was forbidden to investigate any of the conduct of the minister of that department, but was restricted in his investigation to the underlings. Surely, it ill becomes a minister to look for a certificate of character to a commission that was forbidden to investigate anything that might throw any light on his own transactions in the department, or upon his own connection with the delinquencies that existed. We have heard about drowning men clutching at straws, but the anxiety of the Minister of Marine and his followers to obtain a certificate of character for their chief certainly bears a very strong resemblance to that picture. The minister in his defence practically repeats the speech he delivered in this House on April 30, 1908. He goes back and tries to show that the system which is now so much abused by this government was in vogue under Conservative administration. That argument has been very frequently combatted in this House and I do not think it can be combatted too strongly. It does seem to me that the country, and I think most members of this House, are tired of it. Surely the Minister of Marine, surely members on the other side of the House do not pretend to say that a Mr. MEIGHEN.
system that fits one time will fit all times. Surely they do not pretend to say that the successors of the Conservative party for all time to come are to be bound within whatever limits the Conservative party, 20 years ago or 30 years ago saw fit to be bound; surely they would not say that their successors in office for years to come, that their political successors shall have a circle drawn around them and be confined within the narrow limits by virtue of the present administration; surely they will allow some scope for the evolution of political morality and for improvements that will take place. It does not seem to me that it is a sufficient answer to this House and the country that the use of a patronage list in 1886 is a justification for its use years afterwards; surely they ought to make some allowance for the progress of time, surely they must admit that the times have out-grown that system. Supposing they do not admit that, it is not so much the system that is attacked, it is not so much the system that brings disgrace on this government and discredit on its members, as it is the abuse of the system. The abuse of the system seems to have taken root within the last few years. The abuse of this system has not been traced back by Mr. Justice Cassels nor indeed by the previous commission beyond the days of this government. Surely, therefore, they cannot hide behind the fact that the system existed to shield themselves from the consequences of their abuse of that system.
The Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) very rightly suggests that he should not be held responsible for the sins of his predecessors. Personally it would be unjust to hold him responsible. But the Minister of Marine, in common with other members of this government who were members of the government when the minister's predecessor, Mr. Prefontaine, held that portfolio, was responsible for the discrepancies of the Marine Department at that time. I need not take the statements of Conservatives in support of that doctrine of ministerial responsibility, but shall refer to the speeches delivered by prominent Liberals in 1891 when the late Hon. Sir Hector Lan-gevin was charged in this parliament with misconduct in his own department. They will find that one of the strongest constitutional lawyers in this conutry, the late Hon. David Mills, speaking on behalf of the opposition of that day, was very emphatic upon this point. Before quoting his words, let me briefly state the circumstances: The late Hon. Sir Hector Langevin was charged with serious misconduct in connection with the Department of Public Works. Specific charges were made against him. The matter was submitted to a special committee of this House. Two reports were presented to this House, a minority report and a majority report. The majority report specifically

and unequivocally acquitted Sir Hector Langevin from anything in the nature of active participation or any connection with the irregularitites found to exist in the department. The minority report also went so far as to find that they had not evidence to connect Sir Hector with any improper transactions. The two reports coincided in that particular, but the minority report went on-and I draw the attention of the Minister of Marine to this particularly, because they are the words of his colleague in this House, the late Hon. David Mills, and the Hon. Sir Louis Davies of the Supreme Court. At page lxxxii of the Journals of the House of Commons of Canada, A. 1891, appendix No. 1, they say :
Except the desire to please and obey the minister at the head of the department, we cannot discover any motives which would induce these engineers to assist in defrauding the public in order to put money in the pockets of Larkin, Connolly & Co.
Therefore, the ground that these men considered sufficient to connect the head of the department with the frauds perpetrated by those beneath him was that they could conceive of no other motive except that they wished to please and obey the minister at the head of the department. If that ground was good then it is good today, and if it is good now it distinctly implicates the head of the department and puts him on his defence. If the same circumstances exist now as existed then they should lead to the same conclusion.
Speaking in the light of those findings of both the majority and minority reports of those days, Mr. M. C. Cameron, then member for Huron, speaking in the House of Commons of Canada, used the following words at page 5824 of the ' Hansard ':
A member of parliament, a former political friend and supporter of hon. gentlemen opposite, has, for three hours arraigned the policy and the conduct of the hon. gentlemen opposite with respect to their administration of public works, and yet upon the ministerial benches, behind them and on each side of them, there is^ not a man who has courage enough to rise in his seat and defend the position of the government. Hon. gentlemen will remember that this is not an assault solely upon the late member for Quebec West or an assault solely upon the late Minister of Public Works. It is an assault upon every hon. gentlemen who was the colleague of the Minister of Public Works while he was a member of the present administration. They supported and sustained him, and if they know anything about parliamentary, constitutional rule, they must know perfectly well that each one of them is just as responsible as the late Minister of Public Works. I am astounded at the Minister of Justice, and the Minister of War, and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and the Minister of Finance, and above all the Secretary of State, should remain silent in their seats. Are they going to plead guilty to the charges levelled against them?
That is to say, Mr. M. C. Cameron, who was at that time put up by the right hon. gentleman who now leads the government to argue the constitutional aspect of this case as it affected the individual responsibility of the other ministers of the Crown, was made to say and did say that they all shared the responsibility for the guilt even of officials of the department on the ground only as stated in the minority report that there was a reasonable inference that these acts were done either in obedience to their wishes or their orders. As the hour is late I beg to move that the debate be adjourned."]

Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair, I desire to submit to the consideration of this House, and more particularly of the government, a matter which seems to me to be of grave importance to the people of this country, and one upon which I regret to say there is as yet no indication of an intention on the part of the government to take any steps in the direction in which it appears to me such steps are imperatively called for. As this House knows, in 1907 the Civil Service Commission, after making a more or less complete examination into the working of the different administrative departments of this government, submitted a report very severely condemning the workings of one department in particular. This was a department concerning which the commission had made a more careful investigation; but it criticised also other departments with regard to which it expresesd its regret that time had not allowed it the opportunity of making closer inquiry. Upon that report, the hon. the Minister of Marine and Fisheries thought it desirable, in the exercise of the power conferred upon him by statute, to appoint a commission to inquire into the operations of his department. And he appointed the Hon. Mr. Justice Cassels as commissioner to elucidate the question whether or not its officials had so conducted themselves as to deserve the scathing condemnation pronounced by the Civil Service Commission.
In the month of January of this year, the commissioner appointed by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries made his report. That report has been in the possession of the government since some time in J anuary and has also been in the possession of this House for some time; and early in this week we had laid upon the table an order in council in which was set forth the steps which this government had decided to take in consequence of the conclusions reached by the commissioner and set forth in his report.
It is not my purpose to deal in detail with the recommendations contained in that report. To my mind the report is more remarkable for what it ignores than for what it contains. It is more remarkable for what it declines to deal with than for what it has dealt with. While the government has seen proper to deal with some of the questions and with the cases of some individuals in particular condemned by the commissioner, it has kept an absolute silence on some things which are obviously the necessary consequence of the findings

sible minister. Mr. Speaker, I am not here to make any attack upon the honour, nor do I propose to make any appreciation of the conduct of that hon. minister that might reflect upon him in any way. _ _ It seems to me that what his personal position in this matter may be is a question of minor import compared with the greater question to which I would call attention, and in regard to which I only wish it were possible for me to hope that I shall be able to induce action by this government. I take it, as I have said, from the action of the government that they cannot but know that the result of that investigation, the report made upon it, is to establish the possibility that I have indicated, that a permanently established system of corruption should have gone on without the knowledge of the responsible minister, and that in that particular case, it did go on without the knowledge of the responsible minister, and I am not here to question their conclusions in that matter at all.
I am free to say that, in so far as I am concerned in making this motion, I have not risen to make it because of any doubt in my own mind of the personal integrity of the hon. the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. What may be his position_ upon the point of constitutional responsibility is quite another question, and one which, however, I do not propose to touch. But what I do desire to point out is that the action of the government, indicating as it does their belief that this system of corruption, not only could, but did go on without the knowledge of the minister responsible for the administration of that department, conclusively establishes that it is in their judgment possible in this country that such a system may be inaugurated and carried on year after year without the responsible minister having knowledge of it. If that is true, I would ask the ministers who preside over the other great spending departments of this government, and I would ask the right hon. the Prime Minister, who is responsible for all these ministers, and who presides over their operations, whether they are prepared to say that in these particular departments, which have gone uninvestigated, in the face of what has been pointed out by the Civil Service Commission, there is nothing to look into. If the ministers charged with these different departments take the position that under them nothing of this kind can happen without their knowledge, and if the right hon. the Prime Minister approves that position on their Dart, then I say that the government to-day is doing what I have declined to do, and making a direct and most condemnatory attack upon the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. If all these other hon. ministers can sit hack in the absolute eon-Mr. DOHERTY.
spiiousneiss that nothing can go wrong in their departments without their knowledge, it is because they have discovered the secret of watching and supervising all the details of administration. If they take the position that they have been able to do that, then I am at a loss to understand how it is that they condone-because from their point of view it must be something that requires to be condoned-the fact that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries was not able to so control his department that things of that kind could not go on without bis knowledge.	_	_
I am perhaps wasting the time of the House in discussing the question from that point of view. It is manifestly clear that the government recognize the possibility of this state of affairs prevailing in a department without the knowledge of a responsible minister, and as I have said I am not questioning the correctness of that proposition as a proposition of fact. Is it then that these hon. ministers feel that there is something connected with the peculiar operations of the Department of Marine and Fisheries that is of a nature to germinate this corruption and from which their own operations are absolutely tree? Do they think that in their commercial transactions they are dealing with a quality of human nature with which the Department of Marine and Fisheries does not come into contact ? What is the difference in the Department of Militia and Defence, what is different in the Department of Public Works that gives us any reason to suppose that tlieTe would not be the same temptation which we have seen to exist in the Department of Marine and Fisheries, that there would not be the same human nature subject to those temptations, and that there would not be the same succumbing to those temptations that we have unfortunately seen to take place in the Department of Marine and Fisheries ? The responsible ministers of those departments do not need to read between the lines of the report of the Civil Service Commission to see that in the judgment of those gentlemen the system that in their opinion calls for a careful investigation of the operation of a criminal law in England, existed in their (those minister's) departments as well as in the Department of Marine and Fisheries They have no reason, I respectfully submit to suppose that in their operations they may expect any greater immunity from the spirit of graft than has been found in the Department of Marine and Fisheries.	'
But there is more than that. If you go through the evidence and the report of Mr. Justice Cassels you will find evidence that the same men who, in their dealings with the officials of the Marine and Fisheries Department, were guilty of bribery,

have been dealing with the other departments. Is it to be expected that the briber will change his character when he is dealing with one department from that which he has shown when dealing with another? If you consult the returns laid on the table at the instance of the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Sam. Sharpe), you will find the names of a number of people who were proven guilty of bribery in their dealings with the Marine Department figuring as having received large sums of money from each of the other spending departments within the last few years. Was there any reason to expect that the man who would bribe a Marine Department official would be above the idea of trying to cultivate, by irregular means, an official, say of the Department of Public Works or of the Department of Mititia and Defence? You will find in the very report of Mr. Justice Cassels and the evidence of Mr. Halliday, a gentleman who is shown by the report of the honourable judge to have in some very mysterious manner been enabled to be paid by the Department of Marine and Fisheries at the rate of $200 a day, less a rebate I believe of $20, for the use of a vessel which he had contracted to furnish at $125. You will find in that very evidence that, at the very same time, that gentleman was engaged in carrying on a contract for another department of the government of this country and yet that gentleman, as I have said, had managed to receive this extraordinary addition to his contract price from the Marine Department-and nobody can tell the reason why, at least that is the conclusion of the Hon. Mr. Justice Cassels, the commissioner in the matter. A suggestion was made as to the reason why, but the commissioners concluded that that suggestion, which afforded an explanation which would have involved a gentleman more highly placed than any official of the department, was not established. I hasten to say, bearing out what I said in the outset, that the gentleman more highly placed whom I desire to indicate is not the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur). But the remarkable fact remains that that gentleman Mr. Halliday, was dealing at the same time with at least one other great spending department, and that his name will be found in the return to which I have referred as having received very considerable sums of money from the other departments of this government within the period of time covered by that investigation and even since then.
In the report itself you will find evidence as to the dealings of these gentlemen with other departments of this government, and names crop up which are quite familiar to us in connection with certain discreditable transactions that we have heard of in this House and out of the House. If, for in-117
stance, you accompany the commissioner to the city of St. John you will find figuring-not as deserving of words of praise from the commissioner-a name that perhaps might evoke some recollections in the mind of the Minister of Public Works, who, I am sorry to see is not present in the House just now, because these recollections might be most pleasant for him; you will find figuring among the men whose dealings with the Marine and Fisheries Department did not meet the approval of the commissioner, a gentleman who by the present Minister of Public Works during the reign of a preceding minister had been described as being a very nice person to be represented by at Ottawa; the result being that that recommendation and what came of it proved a very nice thing for the gentleman so recommended. And so I say that in the report itself you have intrinsic evidence that these bribers are, or rather have been, in business relations with the other departments of government. I said that the bribers ' are ', but I corrected myself to say that the bribers ' have been ' in business relations with the other departments of this government, because I could hardly invoke the evidence in the report as proof of what has been going on since it was presented. But, outside that report there is evidence which justifies us in concluding that the bribers still are dealing with other departments of this government, and that justification is to be found in ' Hansard ' of March 22 last, in a reply of the Prime Minister to the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe). The hon. member asked:
Has the Marine and Fisheries Department continued to buy supplies, or give contracts to the individuals, supply men, or companies on whose behalf commissions, gratuities or interest were paid to officials of the department, as found by the Cassels commission?
If so, what are the names of such individuals, supply men and companies, and the amount paid or to be paid to them since the receipt of said report by the government?
Have any other departments purchased .supplies or given contracts to any such individuals, supply men or companies since the receipt of said report by the government? If so, what are the names and amounts thereof?
To these questions the right hon. the Prime Minister gave an answer. To the question whether the Department of Marine and Fisheries, or any other department of the government had been continuing to deal with the persons who were found guilty of bribery in the investigation, before Mr. Justice Cassels, the answer of the Prime Minister was :
There may be cases in which it will be in the public interest to do business with some of the parties referred to. Each case will have to be considered on its merits as it arises.
And then, to the question as to the names of these persons and the amount of tha



transactions the government had with them, the Prime Minister gave the oracular reply:
If any particular name be mentioned the information will be given to the House.
Does not that answer come perilously near to saying: 'If you will Just show us that you know all about it why then we will tell you all,' Mr. Speaker. I say that in these answers of the right hon. gentleman we have evidence that justifies us in the conclusion that the men who have been guilty of bribery and found to be so guilty by Mr. Justice Cassels are still considered a worthy class of men with whom, not one department of government in particular but different departments believe they should continue to transact business. The right hon. gentleman tells us that it may be in the interest of the country that the government should continue to give its patronage to the men who have been so convicted; men who have been proven out of their own mouths to have paid bribes to our servants, then added that bribe and Heaven knows what percentage in addition to the price charged to the people of this country, and then pocketed the whole thing to our detriment. And, the Prime Minister tells us in this answer that the attitude of the government towards those bribers remains a matter to be determined in each particular case. Why in England, a man who would be discovered giving a bribe to a public official, would, without any ceremony whatever disappear from the list of those from whom the British government would under any circumstances purchase supplies. I have before me the report of the Public Accounts Committee of the imperial parliament for the year 1907 and I find there two cases which are quite in point to this discussion. One of these cases occurred in the Admiralty Department, and I sincerely trust the inference will not be drawn that there is anything peculiar to Marine Departments or Admiralty Departments which provokes this kind of conduct. In the Admiralty Department it was shown that certain officers had received a commission of five per cent, and by the way I think five per cent was the amount of the commission that played such a large role in the dealings of the Marine Department in Quebec. These officers had received a commission of five per cent upon some clothing purchased by the Admiralty and which it was their duty to pass. And, when the British Admiralty had to deal with that matter they dealt not only with the officials who had received the commission, but they dealt and dealt immediately with the contractors who paid it, and these contractors were at once stricken from the list of persons from whom the government would purchase supplies of any Mr. DOHERTY.
kind. You will find that case referred to at page 4 of the report of the Public Accounts Committee, and you will find it more specifically dealt with in questions from 271 to 280 in the appendix which contains the report of the proceedings. Now, let me call the attention of the House to this, and let us contrast the practice of this government with the practice of the British government under similar conditions. When the question was asked of the responsible minister, if he had determined that the department should cease to purchase goods from the men found guilty of giving bribes, his answer was: 'certainly.' In the report to which I have referred you will find another case in point, and this time it is in the War Department, so that any possible suggestion that there is any particular connection between salt water and this sort of an offence disappears. There was a similar case in the War Department, and when the minister was asked what action he had taken his reply was: 'Why, automatically' - remark the word 'automatically' - 'automatically that man ceases to be a person with whom the government or any of its officials may in future have dealings.' It was not in England, a question of considering each particular case as it is with the right hon. the Prime Minister; it was not considered that it might be in the interests of the country to have dealings with these men; it was not a question of encouraging the man who had been guilty of this despicable crime of bribing his wav into the pockets of the people of the country.
But we need not go to England to learn how men who do that ought to be treated, and whether it is a matter to be dealt with in each particular case. If you turn to our own Criminal Code and look at sections 158 and 159, you will find that every one of these bribers was guilty of a penal offence. We had it some time ago in this House from the lips of a much greater legal authority than I can pretend to be; and if you turn to section 159 of the Criminal Code, you will find that the law of this country has decreed that a portion of the proper penalty to be inflicited upon the man guilty of that offence is that he shall cease to be recognized as having a right to have any contract or any dealing with the government of this country. And yet in the eyes of this government it is a question to be dealt with in each particular case. I say that those answers, indicating as they do a line of conduct that looks upon the action of a briber as something to be leniently dealt with, notwithstanding the letter of the law combined with the terms of those answers, which refused to us in effect information which the hon. gentleman who asked for it and all the members of this House were entitled to

have at the hands of the government, justify us in concluding that to-day the departments of this government are still dealing with these bribers. If we are making any mistake in drawing that inference, I can only say that the responsibility for the mistake lies at the doors of those who refused to us, as they effectually do, this information properly asked for, and lies at the door, too, of the government that has laid on this table the report of what it has decided to do with regard to the report of Mr. Justice Oassels, and has confined itself to telling us simply what it has done or is going to do with regard to certain of its officials, and maintains an eloquent silence with regard to what is going to happen to those political friends, the bribers, whom the report of Mr. Justice Cassels declares to have been guilty, if not more guilty, than the officials who received their bribes. It was this action on the part of the government that led me to say, in opening these remarks, that I regretted that there was absolutely nothing to indicate that this government in the slightest degree contemplated taking steps to investigate the other departments. While in the eyes of this government the bribing of its officials calls for no action so far as the bribers are concerned, the law of this country says that those men should be prosecuted and convicted, and above all should not be dealt with thereafter by the government. I say in all earnestness that I would have welcomed, and would welcome still, from this government, any indication of intention on its part to push through to its proper conclusion this investigation which began with the Department of Marine and Fisheries- to push it through on broader lines, on lines that would indicate an intention on its part to hew to the line, let the chips fall where they may; and if anything that I say now, by way of emphasizing what I consider are the conclusions to be drawn from the inaction of the government, should look as though I were speaking with a desire simply to condemn, I desire to say that all my purpose is to try if I can to bring home to those who are responsible for the conscience of this country the position in which they stand and the responsibility which they are assuming, not by their action, but by their inaction, with regard to what has been established by this commission. Not only is the fact of what has gone on in the Department of Marine and Fisheries in itself sufficient to cause hon. ministers in control of other departments to inquire whether all is well within their households, but we have had the evidence, within the present session of this parliament, of this House putting itself on record as being of the opinion that this sort of iniquity, which we now know to have existed in at least one of the departments of the government, is so generally prevalent throughout the commercial life of this 1171
country, that it was necessary that we should enact a special criminal law to reach it. The government knows that; it knows how prevalent this offence is in the general business of the country; and the inaction of the government leads us to suppose that we are expected to believe that there is no suspicion in the minds of the men responsible for the spending departments of this government that any such thing exists in the course of the immense transactions which some of those departments carry on.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not know that it is necessary that I should dwell at any greater length upon considerations tending to demonstrate the truth of the proposition which I am free to confess seems to me so obviously true. I may say that it seemed to me so obviously true that I have sat in this House since the opening of the session waiting day by day to hear an announcement that this government of its own motion meant to carry the investigation, which had begun in this one department, through to its ultimate conclusion. I am not here to say that such an investigation will necessarily result in the discovery of regrettable facts similar to those which have been brought to light in the Department of Marine and Fisheries. But if such an investigation should demonstrate the entire absence, or even approximately the entire absence of any such corruption in the other departments, that investigation would be worth whatever money it may cost. The people are anxious that matters of this kind should be cleared up. They are interested not merely because of the heavy loss in money, which the prevalence of such a system as has been found to exist in the Department of Marine and Fisheries, must entail, but chiefly because of their desire to ascertain whether, from the highest to the lowest, those charged with the administration of public affairs are perfectly honest, and that the public service of the country may be taken as characteristic of the honesty of the people at large. The people, expect our public service to be of such a character that we need not. when speaking of it, hide our heads in shame. In the report of the commissioner and in the evidence, there are weighty reasons why the government should proceed with such an investigation. Look at the conclusions of that report, and surely the government must pay some attention to the opinion of the distinguished judge whom they selected to make this investigation. What does he tell us is the remedy? You must, he says, rouse the public conscience. Mind you, not the conscience of the employees of the Marine and Fisheries Department, but the public conscience. Why? Because to every reasonable and reflecting man, the evidence leads inevitably to the conclusion that there has grown up among a certain class the belief that the government-not any one department in par-

ticular-but the government as a whole, is fair game and that a legitimate means of making money out of it is to bribe the servants of the country. Then, Mr. Justice Cassels goes on to suggest some other improvements with regard to the Marine and Fisheries Department, and he cannot restrain himself from asking: 'Are there not other departments in which this may be done?' His question implies the suggestion that the conditions in the other departments are similar to what they have been shown to be in the Department of Marine and Fisheries. That is the impression brought home to the public mind by this impartial investigator. I ask the government whether they have any confidence in the man they chose to make the recommendation ? If they have, how can they flout his recommendation? Are they going to sit back and say: 'What is the public conscience to us? We sit in our seats, we hold the reins of power, we may do as we please at all events until another election-what care we for the public conscience? We will satisfy the public by passing a law to prevent the bribery of the servants of individuals, but we will not take any steps to see whether servants of the public are being bribed.' Sir, the government of this country is in a very special manner keeper of the public conscience. I ask you how it is possible to suppress bribery and corruption among our people when we find that those who hold in their hands, for the time being at all events, the control of the destinies of this country, declare that, so far as the departments for which they are responsible are concerned, so far as the business of the people which they are doing is concerned, it does not interest them in the slightest whether the corruption which has been demonstrated to exist in one of the departments does not also exist in the others. Eouse the public conscience, if you will, but our consciences are not to be aroused, would be a fair inference to draw from the inaction of the government.
I do not propose to extend my observations to any further length. The people of this country, I venture to say, look for a thorough investigation of the administrative departments of this government. Such an assertion may not be entitled to any weight coming from myself, and possibly might be questioned, as coming from the opposition benches, but I can support it by authorities which cannot be charged with political bias. Let me cite two quotations from newspapers which support the government and which appeared after the general elections had taken place. These newspapers have told the government in no uncertain tone what I have been trying to impress on the House this afternoon, namely that there is need foT, and this country demands, a thorough investigation into all the spending departments, were it only as an earnest of the sincere intention of this gov-Mr. DOHERTY.
ernment to give us an honest administration of the public business. I read from the Ottawa * Free Press ' of 22nd October, 1908:
Sir Wilfrid's individual strength is great; he has shown on many occasions that he cares for no man. There is an opportunity now for him to prove to the people that they have reason for confidence in him, that not only is he himself a man above suspicion, hut that his whole administration is clean and beyond reproach.
The Liberals as a whole have been classed as a gang of looters.
I am not classing them; I am only reading. *
Sir Wilfrid owes them a clearance certificate.
From what we know of the administration of Sir Wilfrid Laurier in the last twelve years, we believe that it will bear the closest scrutiny; from our knowledge we have been able to characterize as a gross slander the wholesale charges that have been made against it; but there are those not as well informed who are not able to refute the accusations of their fellows, and it is in justice to these men that the most searching investigation should take place, as is now taking place in the Marine Department.
The other I propose to recite is from a newspaper published in the city of Montreal, a newspaper whose devotion-and effective devotion-to the right hon. prime minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and to the party he leads will not be questioned. I read from the Montreal ' Herald ' of 26th October last:-
In the administrative services it is the time for an overhauling and a fresh start. There are departments to which the strong hand must be applied, and people will not be satisfied unless proofs are given that this is understood. Efficiency is demanded and will be insisted upon. At the same time, every reasonable effort to add to the dignity of the service, to minister to the independence and selfrespect of the man who works for the country, will be approved.
And, returning to the charge, on 31st October last, the same paper said:-
Similarly, the Liberal press is not disposed tc take the triumph of Monday last as absolving the party from inquiring if all is well within it. The Ottawa ' Free Press ' demands sn impartial investigation, suoh as is being made into the Marine Department, into the workings of any other department which has come under suspicion. The Toronto ' Globe ' urges the abolition of the patronage system in the purchase of supplies, the reform of the Senate, legislation bettering the conditions of life, the punishment of incompetency and dishonesty in public office, the completion of the scheme of Civil Service reform.
Then, it goes on with its own commentary on what others have said.
All this is good journalism, good partisanship, and good patriotism. The Montreal

' Gazette,' however, sees in it only evidence that the election was won under false pretences. The Liberal press and speakers, it declares, claimed that all the charges of the Conservatives were unfounded, and that the country took them at their word. What a narrow, partisan view. No wonder the Toronto ' Telegram ' claims the ' Gazette ' as a reactionary. No man or journal of any standing in the Liberal party has assumed what the ' Gazette' claims was the general assumption. On the contrary, confession has been made, time and again, that in the spending of millions of money, spread over twelve years, mistakes may have been made. The argument presented to the country, and accepted by it, was that the government, as a whole, was clean and honest; that it had instituted reforms of administration as the necessity developed; that it had ordered independent investigations of alleged evils; that the Premier could absolutely be depended on in every emergency where courage and honesty were required;	
Now, after the conflict, with five years of work before the government, surely it is the part of well-wishers of it, and of the party, to point out the work that is to be performed.
Sir Wilfrid has the ball at his foot as never before. He is under no obligation to any man, or group of men, to refrain from doing as he will along the line of departmental reform, of legislative reform, or of financial retrenchment. In the past he has faced, with courage, and intelligence, and fine public spirit, every issue that presented itself. He has shirked no task, once he saw his duty and his way. Thus he gained that confidence of his fellows so signally defined on Monday. And thus, we may be confident, he will face the tasks that the campaign may have uncovered to his mind. He hais been engrossed for twelve years in the great work of nationbuilding, the work of harmonizing our diverse races, of cementing confederation, of peopling half a continent. Perhaps, for a season, the labours of our Canadian Hercules are to be in a large measure the humbler, but not less necessary, labours of perfecting administration, of safeguarding the public domain from the assaults of the selfish, of creating a healthier public opinion in regard to electoral corruption, and generally in strengthening the moral fibre of the party and the country.
The purpose of my motion is to call upon the government to do the work of generally strengthening the moral fibre, not of the party-I am not so much concerned about that-but of the country. It seems to me that the first step towards that is to make it quite clear that the departments of the government are not afraid to put their operations before the public, but that they are as anxious as the public is, that if there are wrong doings in the operations of those departments, they should be discovered and corrected. And I desire that this should be done, not only so far as the officials of the lower grades are concerned, but from top to bottom of these departments.
I trust that I may be proven to have been mistaken in my view that all the indications were that we need not expect such action on the part of the government. If so, I for one shall hail with pleasure the fact that the government shows itself equal to the task that, it seems to me, clearly lies before it; and I shall be happy to congratulate the government and this country if the result of the investigation should be to show that there was no occasion to make that investigation save in so far as it might serve to relieve the public mind. I hardly venture to hope that that will be the result, but, if it should be, surely the government will not have reason to regret that it made the investigation, and most assuredly the country will congratulate the government and congratulate itself upon such a result having been shown.
But to do that-and I want to insist, just for a moment, on that point-we must have an untrammelled investigation; it must not be a matter of stopping when you strike at the members or when you strike at the man who ' was a member and is a candidate, nor of stopping when you strike at the man whose bribe went as an election subscription, nor of stopping even if you should reach up- which I am not insinuating in any way; it is foreign to my purpose to do so-to the very head of the department himself. To make it worth anything, we must have an untrammelled investigation.
We must not have an investigation that- take one startling instance in this investigation-will make it possible for a government to whom it is reported by an official, a judge entrusted by them to investigate, that an official occupying the highest position in the department under the minister himself, has improperly, at the instigation of two candidates in an election, put 100 men unnecessarily at work upon public work for the sole purpose of influencing their votes-that shall make it possible, I say, for the government, or the minister to whom this report was made, to do absolutely nothing about it. Yet that is what we have in this very report, which is perhaps the most startling instance, or one of the most startling instances of the undesirable effects of the limitation of the power of that commission. Yet I leave it to the common sense of this House if there is any more despicable form of bribery in this world than that which makes the labouring man's bread and butter the price of his vote. I therefore beg to move that all the words of the proposed motion after the word 'that' be left out, and the following be substituted therefor:
That the commission of 1907, in the course of their investigations into the conditions of the Civil Service, having made incidental in-

quiry into the workings of one of the departments at Ottawa, characterized that department as wanting in organization, lacking in conscience, and some of its officials as serving two masters, Scripture notwithstanding, and also criticised other departments.
That the Cassels commission was limited in scope to an inquiry into implied official incompetence and dishonesty in the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and the report thereof with attached evidence simply sustains the charge of official negligence, wastefulness and corrupt dealing in that department, and affords ground for the conviction that similar methods prevail in other great spending departments.
That in order to lift the cloud of suspicion that rests upon the administration of the various departments, to satisfy the demand of the country for honest and businesslike methods, and to purge the public service of inefficiency, reckless waste and corrupt practices, it is advisable and necessary in the public interest that a thorough and untramelled investigation be made by a competent business commission into the workings of all the great spending departments of government.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. P. BRODEUR (Minister of Marine and Fisheries).
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say at the outset that I do not find any fault with my hon. friend (Mr. Doherty) for the way he has presented the case he has just laid before the House; I desire even to offer him my sincere thanks for the personal allusion which he made to me during his remarks. I am exceptionally grateful to him for these kind remarks, because I have not been accustomed in the past to receive that sort of treatment. Ever since I have been in the department I have been doing all that I could to put it upon a proper footing. I was appointed Minister of Marine and Fisheries a few months before the session of 1906, when I had no time to put myself thoroughly au fait of the situation in that department. During that session, several investigations took place in the Public Accounts Committee, and some other committees, concerning the administration of that department. As a result of those investigations, I became aware that some reforms were necessary, especially with regard to the accounting system, which was particularly defective. I appointed some persons who were strongly recommended to me for the purpose of establishing in that department an accounting system which would permit the minister and the superior officers to exercise more effective control over the administration. Later on, when the Civil Service Commissioners came into my department to make an investigation, they may bear testimony to the fact that I gave them the fullest latitude to discover everything which might be wrong in the administration of that department. At last the commissioners reported, stating that:
There would also seem to be a lack of conscience. In connection with the enormous expenditures which are deemed necessary, the Mr. DOHERTT.
word ' discount ' never appears. It is tacitly assumed that there is no such thing; but the whole commercial world knows otherwise. If no one gets any benefit from trade with the government except the trader, then it must be clear that in these great purchases made for the government, without discount, its officers must be assisting the trader to get better prices from the government than he can get anywhere else; for everywhere else he has te give discount. In other words, some of the government's officers are serving two masters, and apparently succeeding with both-Scripture notwithstanding.
I then reported to His Excellency the Governor General and to my colleagues that:
It is assumed by that statement that commissions are received improperly, or enhanced prices paid through dishonesty on the part of the officials of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. But, unfortunately the report does not mention any names which would enable him to take definite action concerning those officials. It is, however, in the interests of the Department of Marine and Fisheries and of the country that immediate steps should be taken in order to determine what officials (if any) deserve condemnation and to give to all an opportunity to meet the charges implied.
That recommendation of mine was concurred in by His Excellency the Governor General and by my colleagues, and the Hon. Mr. Justice Cassels, whom I think everybody in this House recognizes as one of the ablest jurists in this country, a man of impartiality, a man of rectitude, was appointed to discharge the duties of investigating the charges made against the officers of the department. The report is now before us and we have taken action upon it. My hon. friend from St. Anne's (Mr. Doherty) has given us a synopsis of what has been done in connection with officers who were implicated in that report, but now my hon. friend states in his speech that though acknowledging the personal integrity of the minister he cannot fail to say that the minister is constitutionally responsible for the conduct of these officers.
I think what I said was that what the constitutional responsibility might be was a question on which 1 did not want to express an opinion.

As the question of constitutional responsibility has been raised, I may be permitted to say a few words upon it and once for all to lay the responsibility where it should rest, to ascertain whether the minister of the day should be held absolutely responsible for everything that has been done since confederation. Mr. Justice Cassels, in his report, says that the system which has been found defective in the department is mostly the purchasing of supplies, what he calls the patronage system, and he says:

The system seems to have been handed down from one administration to another since confederation.
That is the system which has always prevailed. I shall not take the statement of the hon. judge alone but I think I shall be able to prove to the House by correspondence and documents that the system has also been in vogue when members of the opposite party were in control of the department, and that I was the first minister to make the change which commends itself, to the judgment of Mr. Commissioner Cassels. I have been preceded in the department by a number of ministers, all men of greater ability than I. My predecessors and their terms of office have been:
Ministers.	Dates.
Hon. Peter Mitchell	 1867	to	1873
Smith	 1873	to	1878
Pope	 1878	to	1882
McLelan	 1882	to	1885

Foster	
1885	to	1888Hon. Sir Chas. Hibbert Tupper 1888	to	1894Hon. John Costigan	
1894	to	1896Hon. Sir Louis Davies	
1896	to	1902
Hon. Raymond Prdfontaine.. .. 1902 to 1905
I was appointed at the beginning of 1906. Some of my opponents argue that I should be held responsible for a system which has prevailed under ministers who were very superior in ability to me, but as I have said I was the first minister to get rid of the patronage system in 1908. As this is likely to be the last chapter of this famous marine investigation it may be as well to review what has been done in the past. Let us look at the record since 1867 and ascertain whether I should be held constitutionally responsible for everything which has occurred during that period. In the report of the Auditor-General of 1887, page 393, will be found a letter written by the Auditor General, the late Mr. J. Lome McDougall, to the Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries, on August 21, 1886. In that letter Mr. McDougall said:
I was recently at Quebec and visited the office of your agent there. I find that the supplies purchased by Mr. Gregory are not obtained under contract, and that the prices paid are apparently higher than those which are paid for the same kind of goods for the marine hospital under contract. The differences probably arise from tenders being called for in the latter case and not in the former.
Then the Auditor-General in this letter not only suggests but requests that Mr Gregory should be ordered to purchase his supplies by tender.
Who was then minister?
The hon. member for North Toronto was then minister.
Oh, oh.
Oh come off.

I do not wish to find fault with the hon. member for North Toronto; he was simply doing what other ministers had done before him. My contention is that it is unfair for my opponents to endeavour to charge me with responsibility for every thing which has been brought cut during this investigation when that investigation simply disclosed the same svs-tem as has existed since 1867.
In 1886, then, the Auditor-General requests that tenders be called for. A few months afterwards, on February 21, 1887, Sir Hector Langevin telegraphs to the deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries as follows:
I wish that as usual paint, powder, oils, drugs, common stationery for lighthouses, groceries, hardware and dry goods be purchased in Quebec, also provisions at once.
(Sgd.) HECTOR L. LANGEVIN.
On February 10, 1887, a telegram was sent by the nresent member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) to the deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries, Mr. William Smith, as follows:
Continue usual patronage Baudot & Chinic, Quebec, with conditions as per letter sent concerning Sir Hector's request, inform Caron.
(Sgd.) G. E. FOSTER.
This telegram was signed by the then Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Foster). On the 21st of February, 1887 Mr. Gregory telegraphs to the department as follows:
Navigation nearly open, say whom I am to purchase supplies from and prices to pay. Captains lightships want usual advance. Shall I pay, it takes $2,000.
(Sgd.) J. U. GREGORY.
Here is the memorandum which was prepared by the deputy minister for the then minister:
Please inform me what plan you have decided to adopt about Gregory purchasing supplies, as he does not like to purchase now without authority. The best plan in the public interest is to advertise openly for tenders and let all get a chance to state prices for the principal articles.
21st April, 1887.

Deputy Minister.
Memorandum for the Minister of Marine, relative to the purchase of supplies at Quebec. Immediate.
Mr. McGreevy has handed in the accompanying list of names whom he recommends should receive patronage at Quebec in the purchase of supplies. With reference to the first list marked for tenders he recommends that tenders should be asked from the different parties mentioned therein when any articles are required.
Not public tenders mind you, but simply that tenders should be asked from those

who were political friends of the government of the day, these persons being recommended by Mr. McGreevy the then member for Quebec west.
With reference to the second list he recommends that these persons should be emploved if their services are required, or that supplies should be purchased from them without tender as it would be difficult to make contracts for these articles mentioned in the second list.
(Sgd.) WM. SMITH.
22nd April, 1887.
Minister approves W.S. 23rd April, 1887.
This is a sample of how things were done under the Conservative administration, and if we look at what happened after the member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) left the department we will find that the same system was. perpetuated. In a memorandum from Mr. Smith deputy minister, to the minister on the 27th of October, 1888, he says:
I have visited the different light stations at Anticosti in the government steamer, and while on board the vessel I examined into her internal economy. On inquiry as to prices of provisions it appeared to me that everything was purchased at the fullest market prices, and the captain mentioned to me confidentially that the vessel could be provisioned much cheaper if he would be allowed to purchase in the open market without reference to political patronage.
There had been a change of Minister of Marine in the meantime and this memorandum was for Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper, in 1888, and here is what Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper wrote upon this memorandum:
Arrange a fair rate with each captain accordingly, slightly under existing extravagant system, and have it understood that in the event of complaints being made, if found to be reasonable, fines will be made and deductions from masters' pay for same.
(Sgd.) C. H. TUPPER.
March 11th, 1889.
From this it will be seen that Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper desired to make a change in the manner in which supplies had been purchased and he suggested that a rate should be made with each captain and a contract entered into with him. This system was in force for some years, and after giving the question some consideration I have come to the conclusion that it is certainly the best way in which to provision our vessels; we could contract with the steward or the master of the vessel paying a certain sum of money per head of the crew and no more and no less. But, in 1891 Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper changed this svstem and Mr. Smith the deputy minister in a report to the minister says:
As I presume it is intended to go back to our old system of provisioning the steamers at Quebec, namely, by allowing the agents to purchase the materials as required, and allowing them to use as much as crew wish, Mr. BROUEUR.
but holding the captain and steward responsible for the total average cost per month.
Then he suggested a plan of purchasing supplies from the different firms that were recommended, and letters were sent to Mr. Gregory in Quebec and Mr. Harding in St. John as follows:
I have to request you to invite tenders from a number of friends of the government in the trade for the provisions required during the coming season.
There were to be no public tenders and no public competition, but the purchases were to be made just from friends of the government. Then, I find that on the 4th of May 1891, Mr. Gregory states that he had complied with the instructions, that he had called upon all the friends of the government in the trade to send tenders for the provisions required, that he had consulted Mr. McGreevy and Mr. Chateauvert in order that he might not commit any error in calling on the tradesmen in question, and then he incloses tenders from two or three persons who were friendly to the Conservative government. However, Mr. Gregory was reproached for the manner in which he had done this, and then he answered that there were only two grocers who were friendly to the government and that he could not ask the others to tender because he was told to do business with the friends of the government only. Mr. Speaker, that is the system of purchasing supplies which existed under the Conservative government, and which.has also existed since the Liberal government came in power until last year. Looking at the evidence before us I find, however, that in Montreal from 1888 to 1896 there were only 22 names on the patronage list, whereas from 1896 up to last year there were 170 names on that list, which goes to show that the persons from whom tenders were invited were much more numerous under the Liberal regime than under the Conservative regime. This system as I have shown has existed for many years, but I have come to the conclusion that it should be a system of the past, and last year I changed it and now goods are purchased by public tender in every case where it is possible to do so, without any reference to a patronage list. The system now established is that the purchasing agent should have the right to go not only to friends of the government, not only to my own political friends, but to go any where he wishes in order to obtain the best prices possible in f1'" interest of the country and of the department.
I do not want to find fault with any person in particular for these abuses. The name of my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has been mentioned; but I do not blame him in any shape or form. He simply followed the practice that had previously been in existence. But I ask for myself the same consideration

that I am willing to give to my opponents; I ask to be treated with the same leniency with which I am willing to treat my opponents who were maintaining a system which was bad.

Might I ask the hon. member this question:	If the same thing
took place under a dozen governments before his advent to the department, would that make it less an offence now, that it is continued under his regime, when it is drawn to his attention by his own commissioner?

I am drawing attention to the fact that this system and these abuses have been at all times in existence in the department. At all times it has been represented by officers of the department and by the Auditor General that public tenders should be called for, and that the patronage system should be abolished; and I am glad to say that the first one who had the courage to change that system was myself. My hon. friend will probably one day be a minister of the Crown, and he will then learn how difficult it is to change any system of administration; he will find how difficult it is to eradicate abuses. But I hope he will be able to do his duty, as I know he will be anxious to do it in the best interests of the country. In the meantime, I ask him whether he does not consider that I have done my duty in doing what I have done.

If the hon. gentleman asks me that plain question, I tell him that I do not think he has by any means done his full duty, in face of the report of the commission appointed by himself as one of the ministers of the Crown.

Of course, that is a question of opinion; but when I have had the courage to remove abuses which I have proven existed since confederation, abuses which my hon. friend from North Toronto, one of the ablest men we have in this country, was not able to remove, my hon. friend must admit that the member for Rouville has shown some courage and energy, and has shown that he was willing to discharge his duty.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the work of the department has enormously increased during recent years, and some new and important works have been added to it. We must take that fact into consideration in examining the situation of that department. Take, for example, the services undeT the control of the department; there were 19 twenty years ago; there are now 40, an increase of more than 100 per cent. The expenditure in 1886 was $1,144,520; ten years later it was $1,136,254; last year it was $6,174,855. What caused this great increase? Additional services in the department. I have in my hand a statement showing that the
new services taken charge of by the department since 1896 entailed upon it last year an expenditure of over $2,000,000. These include the St. Lawrence Ship Channel, the dockyards at Esquimalt and Halifax, wrecking plants, the ice breaking steamer at Fort William, wireless stations, a naval militia, marine schools, reporting stations, pilotage, ice-breaking steamers, submarine bells, Parry Sound depot, the lighthouse depot at Prescott. Here are new services that did not exist in 1896, or were not then under the control of the department. If we look at the number of vessels, there were only eight twenty years ago, while there are now fifty-three. Of letters received there were last year 38,190, against 7,800 in 1886, and 13,000 in 1896. Of light stations there were in 1886, 534; in 1896, 629; and in 1908, 957. Of light-keepers, there were 682 in 1886 ; 646 in 1896; 914 in 1908. Of gas buoys there were 39 in 1886 and 470 in 1908. Of wharfs there were 134 in 1886, 416 in 1908. That shows the immense quantity of work which has been added to this department.
How much was dropped in the department when the department was divided into two-the Marine Department and the Fisheries Department?
I am speaking of the whole department-the two branches of the department.
You are practically only dealing with the Marine Department to-day whereas before you dealt with both.

I am dealing with the two branches of the department. They were divided, I think, in 1886, but in 1891 they were brought together again. We have done, I think, some useful work, and in the criticisms to which my department has been subjected, these works have been lost sight of. But I have testimony to the value of what we have done in improving the St. Lawrence. Take the resolutions passed by the Shipping Federation in 1886, 1887, 1906 and 1907. Take those of the Montreal Board of Trade in those late years. I might quote those because they show that something has been done which is very useful. Take the resolution of the 15th of November, 1906, by the Montreal Board of Trade:
Resolved that having received from the president and the representatives of the shipping interests on the council their reports on the annual inspection of the channel, which inspection, by courtesy of the hon. the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, they attended, the council of the Board of Trade of Montreal hereby expresses its appreciation of the manner in which the Dominion government has met the desire of the country that a generous expenditure should be made for the purpose of improving our national waterways from Montreal to the ocean, and the council further expresses its gratitude to the hon. the min-

ister and to the engineers his department for having so readily and promptly met the various specific requests for channel and lighting improvements made by this board and the shipping federation.
Here is the Montreal Board of Trade, the most important body in the country, praising the Department of Marine and Fisheries for what it has done in improving the St. Lawrence route. Take the resolution of the shipping interests of the 21st of November, 1906:
That this federation is extremely gratified with the permanent and substantial manner in which the many undertakings are being carried through and consider that great credit is due to the government and to the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries for the way in which this national work is being done. The beneficial effects have already been felt in the lowering of insurance rates by the St. Lawrence route, which not only benefits the ships, but also the producers in the west.
That the members of this federaton are pleased to note the able manner in which the minister has mastered the many details in the short period in which he has held office.
A resolution to the same effect was passed by the Shipping Federation in 1907:
Be it resolved that the members of the federation express their satisfaction with the permanent and substantial manner in which the many undertakings are being accomplished and consider that great credit is due to the government and to the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries for the manner in which this national work is being carried through.
Those testimonies ought to be worth something. My hon. friend from St. Antoine division (Mr. Ames), who knows the people who have passed these resolutions, will appreciate their value. He knows that they were passed with the desire oi being absolutely true and representing what really existed. I might quote also a resolution from the Board of Trade of Fort William of the 21st of May, 1907, in which they congratulate us for the work we were carrying out at that particular time in connection with the breaking of the ice:
This board fully appreciates the action taken by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries in putting the ice-breaker 'James Whelan ' at work to break the ice blockade on Thunder hay and in the harbour of Fort William this spring. The fact that this breaker opened navigation at least two weeks, and probably three weeks, earlier than_ it would have opened, fully justifies the action of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
That this Board of Trade felt that the work of opening this harbour, so well begun, should he continued each year. The result will he that navigation will open from two to four weeks earlier than it usually does, and such a result is a very important factor in the development of the west, and is of national importance.

What has been the result of our policy and of the work we have been doing on the St. Lawrence? One result has been the lowering of insurance rates to a very considerable extent. On grain these rates have been reduced by 60 per cent of what they were in 1900. On provisions they have been, reduced by 54} per cent, and the president of the Canadian Bank of Commerce, a man who is pretty well posted on all questions concerning finance and transportation, spoke in his speech at the annual meeting of the Canadian Bank of Commerce, as follows:
The Marine and Fisheries Department have also for some years past been steadily improving the lighting of the St. Lawrence, and it is claimed that during the last eight years the decline in insurance rates has been such as to make a saving to freight and vessel owners combined of about $6,000,000.
Here are $6,000,000 which we have saved to the country by improving the St. Lawrence route. Of course during the last elections not a word was said by our opponents about this very beneficial work done by the Department of Marine and Fisheries. They were too busy slandering the minister and his department, for small, petty things, to think of saying a word about the good work we have done in the public interest.
When I took charge of the department, I wanted to make some reforms, and I propose to state in a few words what reforms I have succeeded in making. When the investigation of 1906 took place in the Public Accounts Committee, I found that our system of bookkeeping was absolutely defective. At that time I was told that some changes were being made in the accounting system of the Department of Railways and Canals and that I might get experts who would establish in my department what is called the Cost System. What is that system; it is one by which we can find out in our different stations and places where we manufacture, the cost of each part of a manufactured article. We have not only the cost of the total article but of each part, so that we can easily ascertain whether it will be better for us to continue manufacturing or purchase at the prices elsewhere. Suppose we wanted to purchase anything which pertains to a boiler. What the cost of that part manufactured in one of our establishments was, I could not tell, but by the system I have introduced we can find out exactly what it costs. Then, we can compare that cost with the prices quoted by other dealers and in that way ascertain whether it would be better to continue the manufacture or purchase elsewhere.
That was the reason of the cost system. Formerly, we could not tell whether given parts of the manufacturing articles we were making were too expensive or not. Now, the exact cost to us of manufacturing any part of any article is known to the

officers of the department, and so we can judge whether it is advisable to- continue manufacturing or to purchase. I think the establishment of this system will commend itself to the judgment of the House.
1 found in the department a system, which had been in existence for many years by which there could be overlapping payments-in other words, the expenditure in each year was not kept within the appropriation. I do not remember exactly the amount paid out of the appropriations oi 1905-6 on account of expenditures incurred in the previous year, but I know that the amount was a very large one. I thought this system extremely detrimental to the administration of the department, and decided to change it. Within a few weeks after I took charge of the department, I instructed the proper officers to see to it that each officer under whom expenditures were made should make a statement showing exactly what he required to complete the expenditures of the year, and what money remained to meet these requirements. I was very sorry to find that, in the first report laid before me by Mr. Falconer, no less than $484,000 was paid during 1906-7 for expenditures incurred in the previous year. My hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) knows what abuses such a system can bring about. Being determined to change this system, I gave such formal and unmistakable instructions that now, to-day, on this first day of April, 1909, at the opening of the fiscal year, I am in a position to state that all the expenditures incurred in the fiscal year closing yesterday can be paid out of the appropriations for that year. I have here a monthly statement such as I get from my officers regularly, showing the amount of each appropriation, the amount spent during the month, the total amount spent to date and the balance available. Not only expenditures for the current fiscal, but also those made on account of last fiscal year must be clearly shown. With such a statement before me, I am able to judge whether there will be enough money to provide for the necessities of the year. 1 can completely control every expenditure, and can see whether each officer is living up to my instructions or whether he is transgressing those instructions. The report I have now in my hand is that of March 1, 1909. It shows that, on appropriations representing a total of $7,055,600, there was a balance available of $1,870,000, or enough to cover all the expenditures to be incurred during that year. This method enables me to absolutely prevent overlapping payments, a system which, perhaps, led to the abuses which were discovered in Quebec. Such abuses cannot occur under the system I have established. As a part of this system, I have a statement prepared
by my officers, every month showing the amount of the appropriation and the amount expended and the balance available. For the fiscal year, 1908-9, the year which closed yesterday, is a balance of our appropriation of $883,000_that will not be required. In other words, there will be no overlaping payments for the fiscal year just closed.
Another reform that I made in the department was the classification of the lighthouses. I found that the salaries of the light-keepers were graded, not according to the work they had to do, not according to the importance of the lights they had to take care of, not according to any good business principles which should guide in such cases, but according to the favoritism a man might be able to claim, according to his influence, sometimes even according to the number of children he had. I thought that was a system that should be put an end to, and so I asked my officers to make a classification of all the lights according to their importance, according to their sites, according to the illuminating apparatus installed in them, in order that the salaries of these light-keepers should not be purely and simply at the discretion of the minister but should be regulated according to business principles. I did the same thing in the classification of the fog alarms, no such classification having existed up to that time.
I come now to another reform-the fifth -which I consider I have introduced in the department: the appointment of a purchasing agent. Abuses have been proved by the investigation to have existed because purchases were made without much consideration for the price, sometimes without much consideration for the quality or even the quantity of goods. I thought that we should centralize these purchases, and that local parties should not be the only ones to quote our prices. However, in order to protect the local dealers, to-day, when we advertise for goods we always state, if these goods have to be delivered at Quebec, Halifax, St. John or elsewhere, that tenderers shall quote prices for goods delivered at the point selected. The results have been very satisfactory. We call publicly for tenders in all cases where the amount is large enough to justify us in doing so. In all cases of purchases exceeding $5,000 we call in this public way for tenders. For smaller purchases, the purchasing agent is absolutely free to go where he likes to make these purchases, his instructions being to get the lowest prices and the best conditions possible.
Also , some two years ago, I abolished the free importation of goods, because I found there were abuses in connection with that system. Even before a law was passed by parlia-

ment declaring that goods purchased by government should pay duty, I gave instructions that goods, purchased in my department should pay duty, and consequently I do not think that we will experience any longer the same troubles that were disclosed, in some cases, by the investigation.
