The contract system has been established on the boats, and now we have given contracts for supplies on all the boats of the government, with one or two exceptions. Last year my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) discussed this very question, and urged that it would be a good thing to provision the boats, not by purchasing the goods ourselves, but by making contracts through the captains and stewards of those boats. That system is now in vogue, it was in vogue even when he drew my attention to it on several of our boats, and at present the contract agent is completing arrangements for the other boats we have. I think I may also mention the great improvement that has taken place with regard to the works under the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal. My hon. friend from St. Anne, Montreal, (Mr. Doherty), knows very well how those works were carried on previously in the Montreal harbour. A new commission has been appointed, and now the work is being done in a way which is creditable, not only to the commissioners, but to the whole country.
My hon. friend from St. Anne states that corrupt acts have been committed; it is true. He states that corrupt acts have been disclosed; it is true. But let me assure him that these corrupt acts were unknown by .the minister or by any of the superior officers of the department. Those acts took place under a system which had been in vogue for many years, a system which had not given satisfaction, and a system which we are now changing. I do not desire to prolong my remarks. I think I have shown that the Department of Marine and Fisheries is now on a footing which will commend it to parliament and to the country. Should we go further? My hon. friend says we should go further, and make a further investigation. In all cases there is not the same justification as there was in the Department of Marine and Fisheries. Does he want to have all the officers branded as robbers? Does he want all the officers of the government branded as thieves, or as having received gratuities? I know he does not want that. We must take it for granted that these officers are honest. There was justification for an inquiry in the Marine and Fisheries Department, because we had before us the report of the Civil Service Commis-Mr. BRODEUR.
sioners, in which they stated that there was a lack of conscience in the department. But I do not think my hon. friend is justified in going any further.
Now, some allusion has also been made to the dismissal of officers from my department. I must say, Mr. Speaker, that it was a very painful duty for me to perform. I received a great many letters, supplications from mothers, sisters, wives and children, imploring me to show compassion on those who had been implicated in the disclosures of the Cassels investigation. I did find that in some cases it was very hard to resist the appeals of these persons. But I approached the matter, neither with antipathy nor with sympathy, but with the sole desire of rendering justice to all those who were the subjects of the investigation. I have tried to do my duty, not as an enemy, not as a friend, but purely and simply as a judge in the discharge of his duty. The report on this matter, which was laid before the House a few days ago, was a result of the mature judgment and consideration of all the cases of men who were implicated in those disclosures. I think, Mr. Speaker, that in doing this I have only fulfilled my duty, as I was bound to fulfil it, in view of the disclosures which were made. Finally, I place myself in the hands of parliament. I am ready to submit to the judgment of the country, and it is my belief that the country will see the Department of Marine and Fisheries conducted in future in such a manner that is will be at all times a credit to this country.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. W. MADDIN (South Cape Breton).
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the resolution which has been placed in your hands, moved by the hon. member for St. Anne, Montreal, (Mr. Doherty), has for its object to impress upon the government the necessity of making an inquiry into the other spending departments of this government, such as has been made into the Department of Marine and Fisheries by His Honour Mr. Justice Cassels. In fact, the resolution goes further than that, it suggests a searching, untrammelled and a more thorough inquiry than that which was held by Mr. Justice Cassels. The hon. the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, after occupying the attention of the House for something more than an hour, endeavouring to answer the arguments of my hon. friend from St. Anne, has not succeeded in answering one of them. During nearly the whole of his speech he seemed only anxious to defend himself, and to make out for himself a good character in respect of his administration and the efficiency of his department. He appeared to be very anxious to exhibit the endorsations

which he had received from various boards of trade throughout the country. Sir, in that respect	his	department is not	inquestion in this resolution, nor is it before the	House	at the	present time.No one	at	this	time is	making	anycomplaint that his department is not efficient,	no	one	on this	side of	theHouse denies that improvements have been made in his department. That might be said at another time and under other circumstances; that aspect of the minister's department is not now before the House. The question before the House is simply this:	Do we learn sufficient from the report submitted to us by Mr. Justice Cassells to warrant us in taking the public behind the scenes in the other great spending departments of this government? The Minister of Marine has not offered one reason why such an investigation should not be had. He asks that his conduct in the department should be condoned and points out that he is the least of a great number of men who have filled that office, and then he tries to show that he was the one man of all these who had the courage to boldly come out and undertake reform. He tells us that he was appointed Minister of Marine in February, 1906. On May 8, 1906, only a few months after the hon. gentleman undertook the duties of that office, the member from Grenville (Mr. J. D. Reid) in addressing the House, spoke as follows:-
Up to about two or three years ago, we had the Pintsch gas system by which we had a permanent light on the gas buoys. It was changed then to the acetylene gas system.
Further on he says:
I have not the slightest hesitation in saying, as I see from the Auditor General's report, that the government have spent in the neighbourhood of $1,000,000 in the fiscal year of 1905 in making these changes, that there has been a very considerable rake-off, say from 25 to 50 per cent. Some one is getting that rake-off. There is a system going on in the Marine and Fisheries Department by which, on almost every item in connection with this matter, there is a rake-off of at least 25 per cent, and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, when he examines the accounts that go through his department, will have to come before the House and admit that there is 25 per cent at least paid on every item in connection with this matter over and above what I or any other member of this House could purchase these appliances for. That is a fact, and I defy the minister to dispute it. I can prove it here by the items in the Auditor General's report. It is most unfair to have a system of that kind going on in the Marine and Fisheries Department. It is not going on without some one getting a rake-off. We should know who is getting that rake-off! It is a shame that this oountry has to pay these exorbitant prices.
This was in May, 1906. Yet the Minister of Marine boasts here of the virtue in his
department. When a woman boasts about her virtue we at once become suspicious. The minister did not waken to his sense of duty until in 1908 he says he had the courage to order goods to be purchased in his department by public tender. Further than that, after the hon. member for Grenville (Mr. J. D. Reid) brought this matter to the attention of the Minister of Marine, a new system of bookkeeping was introduced into that department at the instance of the minister; at a very great expense to the people of this country, Falconer & Co. of New York made a searching inquiry and audit of the books of the Marine Department. What did they discover? They discovered a system prevailing there that was even worse than Mr. Reid in his modesty had suggested. Although this investigation took place in 1907 the minister undertakes no reform until 1908. The minister says that from the earliest time in this department of the government the system of buying goods through government patronage has obtained and after doubtless searching the records of the department with the greatest care he brings here a letter written in 1886 and points out that it is shown in that letter that when the hon. member for North Toronto was Minister of Marine and Fisheries, the purchase of supplies at Quebec was under the patronage system, that the sale of supplies for the St. Lawrence branch of the Department of Marine and Fisheries was not open to the public but was circumscribed to the extent that purchasers were obliged to buy from certain Conservatives whose names were put on the patronage list. For years preceding 1896 hon. gentlemen opposite were wont to go to the country and point out amongst other evils which characterized the Conservative administration that of the patronage system. They boasted on every platform that when they got into power they would abolish that system forever. In that way they obtained the confidence of the people and were entrusted with the administration of the affairs of the country and why did they not then bring about these reforms? It ill becomes the Minister of Marine in 1909 to say that because in 1886 a system obtained which was bad the government were justified in carrying on the same system. Two wrongs cannot make a right and the minister's statement that this system obtained in the past does not by any means exculpate his department and the present administration.
At six o'clock, House took recess.
After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

When you left the chair at six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I was referring in detail to some of the instances disclosed

by this report of the Cassels commission. We find that a man named Wm. Blackeson, who followed the occupation of his father as a sail maker, testified that he paid five per cent commission to Mr. Gregory as his father had done before him. Mr. J. J. Murphy paid five per cent commission to Mr. Gregory, and Mr. Murphy received 15 per cent profit on his sales to the government over and above what he paid Gregory. We find also that no less than 28 officials of the department in the city of Quebec received from Mr. Drolet a sum of $9,342 in a period of three years, an average of $3,114 per year, on an average per head of $111 for these 28 men. Then we have it in evidence that Mr. P. J. Mailloux knew of payments being made to Mr. Gregory, and that George Davie of the firm of Davie & Sons paid Gregory $500 per year on an average for eleven years, in addition to paying $75 to Mr. Petty, engineer of the ' Montcalm.' Mr. Davie, who had large contracts with the department, well knew that in receiving these payments Gregory was violating the law of the country, and hc\ doubtless also knew that he himself was guilty of an offence because he admits that he departed from the ordinary custom of his business, and, in order, as he says, to shield Gregory, he took the extraordinary course of drawing the $500 on McGee & Company, brokers, and having it paid in five-dollar American green-back bills so as to leave no record of the payment. This man also testifies that a further sum of $800 was paid to Mr. Gregory on August 30, 1906, and a still further sum of $500 was paid to him in August, 1907. This same man Davie was making a profit of 50 per cent on his contracts with the department. Among other favours conferred on Mr. Gregory by Mr. Davie the latter paid Gregory $400 to go to New York to transact some business for him, and it developed that he was paid this sum to use his influence as a government official to assist Mr. Davie in selling some dredging apparatus to an American firm. In addition to this, in December, 1907, Mr. Davie paid the captain of the La Canadienne $25; in December, 1906, $50, and in 1905, meeting him on the street one day, he casually handed him a one hundred dollar bill. Here are specific instances in which a briber approached the officers of the government and bribed them, not with trifling sums, but with sums aggregating more than a year's wages for most of the artisans and labouring men of the Dominion. An artisan who averages $800 per year thinks he is well off, and yet on one occasion this lump sum was paid by one contractor to this official of the government. The evidence with regard to the Hallidav Bros, is a striking illustration of how things were manipulated at Quebec. Thev had a contract with the government for the services of the S.S. ' King Edward' by which originally they Mr. iMADDIN.
were to be paid $135 a day, and these men were receiving pay from another department at the same time they were under contract with the Marine and Fisheries Department. They subsequently rendered a bill to the Marine Department for $200 a day for the steamer, and eventually they were paid at the rate of $180 per day or $45 per day more than the original contract. A Mr. George B. Hall handed Mr. Gregory a gratuity of one hundred dollars, and although Mr. Hall is a lumber merchant, yet he was selling oil to the department and making a rake-off from 25 per cent to 30 per cent as a middleman in that business. Mr. Wm. Doyle paid Mr. Gregory a commission of 3i per cent or $495 on $17,300 worth of goods which he sold to the department. It seemed that Mr. Gregory owed Mr. Doyle $613.90, and that account was wiped out by Gregory paying Doyle $117.77. Mr. Drouin allowed Gregory five per cent on the purchases which Gregory made from him for the department, the scheme being that Gregory paid the amount to Drouin previous to the receipt of the government cheque and this five per cent was said to be by way of discount. Then, Mr. Gillespie also borrowed from Gregory so as to allow him five per cent. I shall not go further into minute details in connection with this matter, but I do wish to draw the attention of the House to the fact that section 158 of the Criminal Code, was framed to meet such cases. Section 158 reads as follows:
Every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to a fine of not less than one hundred dollars, and not exceeding one thousand dollars, and to imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year and not less than one month, and in default of payment of such fine to imprisonment for a further time not exceeding six months who-
(a)	makes any offer, proposal, gift, loan or promise, or gives or offers any compensation or consideration, directly or indirectly, to any official or person in the employment of the government, or to any member of his family, or to any person under his control or for his benefit, with intent to obtain the assistance or influence of such official, or person to promote either the procuring of any contract with the government for the performance of any work, the doing of any thing, or the furnishing of any goods, effects, food or materials, the execution of any such contract, or the payment of the price or consideration stipulated therein, or any part thereof, or of any aid or subsidy payable in respect thereof; or,
(b)	being an official or person in the employment of the government, directly or indirectly, accepts or agrees to accept, or allows to be accepted by any person under his control or for his benefit, any such offer, proposal, gift, loan, promise, compensation or consideration ; or,
(e) being an official or employee of the government, receives, directly or indirectly, whether personally or by or through any member

of his family or person under his control or for his benefit, any gift, loan, promise, compensation or consideration whatsoever, either m money or otherwise, from any person whomsoever, for assisting or favouring any individual in the transaction of any business whatsoever with the government, or who gives or offers any such gift, loan, promise, compensation or consideration; or,
[DOT](g) having dealings of any kind with the government through any department thereof, pays to any employee or official of the government, or to any member of the family of such employee or official, or to any person under his control or for his benefit, any commission or reward or within one year before or after such dealings, without the express permission in writing of the head of the department with which such dealings have been had, the proof of which permission shall lie upon him, makes any gift, loan, or promise of any money matter or thing, to any such employee or other person aforesaid; or
(h) being an employee or official of the government, demands, exacts or receives from such person, directly or indirectly, by himself, or by or through any other person for Ms benefit, or permits or allows any member of his family, or any person under his control, to accept or receive (i) any such commission or reward, or (ii) within the said period of one year, without the express permission in writing of the head of the department with which such dealings have been had, the proof of which permission shall lie upon him, accepts or receives any such gift, loan or promise.
Now, I wish to read section 159:
Every person convicted of an offence under the last preceding section shall be incapable of contracting with the government, or of holding any contract or office with, from, or under it, or of receiving any benefit under any such contract.
I have read these portions of section 15S which are pertinent to this resolution and the whole of section 159, in order to emphasize to this House that in 1892, and I doubt not previous to that, there were provisions in the Criminal Code of this country for the punishment of the identical offences which Mr. Justice Cassels has found to be so rampant in the Department of Marine and Fisheries. I do this to emphasize the fact that the criminal law of this country was framed and passed in order to meet just such cases as have arisen here. This report of Mr. Justice Cassels came down in the latter mirt of Januarv. and on the first day of February a Bill, entitled 'An Act to prevent the payment or acceptance of illicit or secret commissions and other like practices.' received its first reading in this House. The first section of that Act is as follows:
This Act may be cited as 'The Secret Commissions Act, 1909.'
When that Bill was introduced into this House by the hon. the Minister of Justice,
while agreeing with him that the provisions contained in it would meet with the approval of a majority of the people, I endeavoured to point out that it was most desirable that the criminal law of this country should be preserved in the codical form in which it had been handed down to us by the late Hon. John S. D. Thompson; so that we should have our criminal law in one volume and not distributed through the various statutes of Canada under different headings, and with various high-sounding titles. Was there any special motive for introducing that Bill at that particular time? As up to that time there had been no persons prosecuted under the Criminal Code for receiving secret commissions, was it hoped that the people throughout the length and breadth of the country would, by the introduction of that Bill, have their eyes closed to the lack of prosecutions by the government for the flagrant disclosures made in the report of Mr. Justice Cassels? When it became known that that report would bristle with the most flagrant instances of violations of the criminal law of the country, it was sought to draw a red herring across the trail, by introducing a piece of legislation which, although it does not on its face say so, implies that it was framed for the purpose of meeting any future cases that might arise similar to those disclosed by the investigation into the affairs of the Marine and Fisheries Department. The criminal law of the country is quite clear with regard to these offences. I have read what sections 158 and 159 of the Code have to say, and I can readily appreciate the sentiments in the mind of the hon. the Minister of Marine and Fisheries when he says that no one knows how hard it was for him to apply the pruning knife to his department, to the extent he did, as shown by the order in council brought down the other dav. I can readily understand how, moved by letters addressed to him from the wives, mothers, sisters, and children of officials in his department, he is loath to institute prosecutions against them. I would not for a moment advocate that an example should be made in every individual instance in which an offence has been disclosed by this investigation; but I say this, that when it comes to the knowledge of a community or a country that a part of the criminal law of the country has been openly and flagrantly violated for a period covering several years, it bpcomes the duty of the person responsible for the administration of the department in which these crimes arose, to make an example of someone ;-to single out some of the more flagrant instances-and there are many-and institute proceedings against the parties. The hon. Minister of Marine and Fisher-
Will the hon. gentleman be kind enough to quote one instance when I said anything of the kind.
I am not prepared to state on what platform or on what day the hon. minister said it, but I promise him that I will furnish him with the place and date.
I never said anything of the kind.
In deference to the hon. minister and to the rules of the House I am obliged to accept his denial, but I was told this on the authority of members from the province of Ouebec.
Name them.

I do not propose to name them. They are not on that side of the House at any rate. This was the reason put forth by the French-Canadian press in the province of Quebec to account for the attacks made on the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. Let me say that the Liberal-Conservative party has never been found wanting in regard and esteem for French-Canadians. That, narty, from the beginning of confederation, and long previous to confederation in Upper Canada, held the French-Canadian people in the highest esteem. Hon. gentlemen on this side are always willing to nay any tribute due to the memory of Champlain and Cartier and even to the right hon. the leader of the government, in so far as he is a Canadian citizen. We have never been lacking on this side in regard for our compatriots of French origin, so that it cannot be said, with any degree of truth, that it was be-Mr. MADDIN.
cause of the hon. minister's origin, he and his department were attacked.
Let us trace the history of this investigation. A commission was appointed and this commission reported in 1907, and in its report reflected on the administration of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. The hon. minister then suggested this inquiry. urged on by his colleagues in the cabinet. It was they who instituted these proceedings, and for any disclosures which have arisen, they have only themselves to thank. But the resolution moved this afternoon has for object an inquiry into the other spending departments of the government; and unless hon. gentlemen opposite support this resolution, it may be said, with some degree of truth, that the Marine and Fisheries Department was made the scapegoat for the sins of the other departments as well as its own. Unless this resolution be accepted by the government, they must consider that the Department of Marine and Fisheries is better administered than the others. After the mover of this resolution (Mr. Doherty) had addressed the House this afternoon, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries rose to reply; and I venture to say that this is the first instance in the history of confederation, when a minister of the Crown replied to a resolution without committing himself either to an endorsement of it or to opposing it. He did not intimate how he proposed to vote if the House came to a vote on the question. He did not say that he was opposed to the resolution or that he approved it; but by inference, perhaps, it may be concluded that he does not intend to support it. The hon. minister _ went back through the history of the Liberal-Conservative party looking for precedents. It is remarkable how, when this government wishes to find a precedent for anything that will hardly bear close scrutiny, it always endeavours to find one in the past records of the Liberal-Conservative party. Well, after going through the records of that party from 1878 to 1896, one letter was discovered written in 1886.
Why, asked the minister, do not my opponents give me credit for the great results I have accomplished, for the good I have done? But on the other hand, why does not the minister play fair? Why does he not give credit to the then Minister of Marine for the good things done under the Liberal-Conservative party in the eighteen years they were in power? Instead of looking up ancient history, why does not he apply himself to something more modern and look through the correspondence on the files, from 1896 to the present, regarding expenditures of Whe character described in Judge Cassels' report? If he had any desire to act fairly, he would do that, but evidently he has no such intention.
In conclusion, I have only to observe that the minister has not met the issue

raised in this resolution, but has simply contented himself pointing out the reforms undertaken and carried out by his department. He has argued in a most peculiar fashion, and made some very illogical deductions. In effect, he says. 'Under my administration I have improved the St. Lawrence service, as you will see by resolutions passed by the Quebec Harbour Commission; I have introduced ice breakers, and call your attention to the resolution adopted by the Board of Trade of Port Arthur. I have caused the rates of insurance to be reduced on the St. Lawrence route; I have introduced a new system of bookkeeping in the Department of Marine and Fisheries; and because I have done all these things there should be no inquiry into any other spending departments of the government.' Would any one call that a logical argument? In his report Mr. Justice Cassels states that in order to bring about a successful reform in the spending departments of the government, it was advisable to awaken the public conscience. Why then will not the government accept this resolution? Have they anything to fear from it or to lose by it? Does the government consider that suspicion, as a result of this Cassels inquiry, is not deeply rooted in the public minds? If the other spending departments of this government are above reproach, an inquiry will redound to the credit of the administration, and I believe that there is no member on this side of the House but will be only too happy to find that there was no ground for such an inquiry. But that the circumstances demand that the inquiry be made, I think no reasonable man can deny. Why, what would be thought of a business man, say Mr. Thomas Lindsay, of the city of Ottawa, who runs the department store down town, if he, upon investigation, found fifteen or twenty people trading with the clerks in his grocery department had been bribing those clerks with thousands and thousands of dollars which they had added to the price of goods which they sold to the department, and, though these identical men were doing business with his millinery department, his furniture department and other departments, should still say: ' Oh, it's all right; I will not inquire into these other departments; probably everything is straight there '? Do not you suppose that under such circumstances any business man would at once investigate every department under his control? And do not you suppose that, in any event, he would at once cut off from the list of those with whom he transacted business the names of persons whom he found guilty of corrupting the employees under his control? Will the government follow the counsel of this commission and make an endeavour to awaken the public conscience? Or are they afraid that they may awake the wrong passenger, that they 118
may awake public indignation?-that they fear that an investigation into the other spending departments of the government would not redound to the credit of their administration? I wonder if the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham), the Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden), the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley), the Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux), the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver), and the Minister of Mines (Mr. Templeman)-I wonder if these gentlemen were to take the evidence submitted by Mr. Justice Cassels in his report and make a careful perusal of it, if they would not recognize the names of those who have corrupted officials in the Department of Marine and Fisheries as the names of those who are still doing business with their several departments. For the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to argue that this system of patronage obtained under Liberal-Conservative rule is no justification. In his perusal of the files in his department from 1896 to date, he does not show us any instances such as the dozen or more that I cited to him here to-night; all that he does show-and I suppose he has shot his bolt, that he has selected that specific case which he thought would apply here -is that a system of competition by which the late government practised the custom of buying from friends of the administration. They bought by tender from amongst the supporters of the Liberal party who were on the patronage list of the government. But still there was competition among the supporters of the government to get the contract whatever it might be. That is entirely different from the condition that has obtained under the present government up to this time. I submit that it is one matter to have a patronage system where goods are bought in competition between friends of the government and an entirely different matter to have a system under which friends of the government are put up to compete against each other, the contract to go to the one who will give the highest bribe to the ofiicials. I say that in view of the evidence submitted in this report showing the relation of these bribers to this department and other departments (the significance of the report being as much in what it does not say as in what it does say), and in view of the circumscribed nature of the commission which Mr. Justice Cassels had which would not let him go beyond certain means and abuses, taken under these circumscribed conditions,_ it is of such a character as not only requires but demands the fullest and most untrammelled inquiry that the government can hold.
I desire to offer one or two observations touching the matters that have been discussed this afternoon in connection particularly with the report of Mr. Justice Cas-

seia in his investigation into the Department of Marine and Fisheries. I presume that there will be no question on the .part of gentlemen on either side that it is in the highest degree desirable that the very best officials, the most competent and honest men, the most trustworthy men, should be employed by every department of the government throughout the whole country. I think that every hon. member will agree that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur), like every member of this government, is not anxious to retain in the employ of the government men who are guilty of a breach of trust or of violating the sacred honour reposed in them in respect of their employment. But we must not lose sight of the fact that the government of Canada is a large institution, that it employs a horde of officials from one end of this broad Dominion to the other, that these employees are not brought directly under the supervision of the minister responsible for their actions, and it naturally occurs- it must inevitably occur- that much must depend on the personal integrity of the men so employed. It has happened that certain officials of the Marine and Fisheries Department have been proven guilty of wrongdoing and of neglect of that standard of honesty and rectitude set up for the guidance of public officials. The question is not whether the government has acted faithfully in carrying out its trust in this matter-the charge is not made that the government or any department has not dealt out summary punishment to those officials when any wrong-doing was brought to their notice. The report of Mr. Justice Cassels deals with a number of officials in Quebec, in St. John, in Halifax, who have been more or less derelict in respect to their obligations to the government and of the code of honour which they should apply to their own conduct. We have before us an order in council submitted by the First Minister a couple of days ago in which is recited what has been done with respect to the officials thus wanting in their duty and honesty. One would think, from the address of the hon. member for Ste. Anne (Mr. Doherty) and the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr Maddin), that the government, having learned that its officials had been derelict in their duty or guilty of breach of trust, instead of summarily punishing them had condoned the offences of which they were proven guilty. That is not the case. The evidence before us in respect of that ( order in council goes to show that every | official who was guilty of wrong-doing has i been punished in the manner called for by ! the obligations of the government in this I regard. I am not going to enumerate the t names of those officials, because I think it i is not desirable that their names should be < embalmed on the public records of this < country. I will merely repeat, that every Mr. KYTE.
one of those officials who has been proved guilty of dishonesty has been dismissed, and they are no longer in the employment of the government.
Now, with respect to the ministers themselves, I beg to remind the hon. gentleman that there is not one single word censuring any member of the government, in the whole of this inquiry and report of Mr. Justice Cassels. I am well aware, and the House is well aware, that for the past twelve months the atmosphere resounded with all kinds of charges of wrongdoing and wholesale corruption in respect of the various departments of this government. During the last election campaign we remember that every minister was put upon his trial, and charges the most flagrant and most unjust were levelled against them. But the report of the commissioner exonerates absolutely every minister whose name was dragged into this question. Inasmuch as the hon. member for St. Anne devoted a great deal of attention to the report of the Civil Service Commission, I wish to call attention to the fact that that commission did not examine any person upon oath. They had a commission to inquire into certain departments of the government, and as a result of that inquiry, not based upon any sworn testimony, they came to the conclusion that there were certain things transpiring in some of the departments that were not desirable. Referring to their strictures in respect to the light house board, on page 8, Judge Cassels says:-
I am quite satisfied that had Messrs. Fyshe and Bazin heard the evidence adduced before me, the language quoted above would not have been used by them.
That is, language referring to certain maladministration with respect to the Lighthouse Board, in which wrong-doing or want of conscience, as they put it, was charged. But, as I said a moment ago. Judge Cassels having heard the sworn testimony of every person giving evidence, came to the conclusion that if these gentlemen had heard the sworn evidence adduced before him, they would not have used that language. With respect to their references to other branches of the Civil Service, I desire to point out that the commissioner does not censure the minister of any one of the departments of the government. As a matter of fact, the Civil Service Commission does speak of the Post Office Department, the Department of Railways and Canals, the Department of Customs and the Department of Secretary of State, but in terms which do not at all imply that they had discovered the slightest trace of wrong-doing. The only two departments referred to at length by the commission were the Department of Marine

and Fisheries and the Department of Militia and Defence. Let me refer for the moment to the statement with respect to the Department of Militia and Defence. The only charge made against that department is the charge that they were spending a great deal of money, and this is what the report says:-
The expenditure in this department is going up hy leaps and hounds. In 1903-4 the total expenditure, both in capital and consolidated fund, was in the neighbourhood of three and a half million dollars. In the estimates lately submitted to parliament for the fiscal year ending March 81, 1909, appropriations are asked for aggregating $6,500,000. That is to say, in four years and three-quarters the expenditures will have increased, if the supply asked for is granted, to the extent of three million dollars.
Now, that in itself does not imply any wrong-doing in the Department of Militia, though one might be inclined perhaps to suppose that the commissioners had in mind some suspicion that money was improperly spent. I need scarcely remind you that within the period referred to by the Civil Service Commission during the last four years the Department of Militia and Defence, in pursuance of that policy of expansion and with the object of relieving the mother country of some of the burdens that she bore for a hundred years in our defence, came to the conclusion to assume the maintenance of the fortifications at Halifax and Esquimalt. Hon. gentlemen opposite are loyal to the British empire, are loyal to the flag of Great Britain, and we had evidence a few evenings ago of what these hon. gentlemen think of Canada's duty to aid in the defence of the empire. Surely, then, those hon. gentlemen will not censure the government because the expenditure in the Militia Department has increased two or three million dollars by reason of the added responsibilities assumed by that department in taking over these fortifications. It is a fact that the estimates of the department were increased by over two millions on the single item to maintain the garrison at Halifax, but surely no hon. gentleman opposite will find fault with the department for undertaking this expenditure, inasmuch as by so doing they are relieving the mother country of a great burden. Now, with respect to the internal management of the Militia Department, they do make some criticisms of certain officials, and of the duties assigned to them, and they point out that perhaps in some respects the expenditure might be decreased and greater economy practised if that department were reorganized. Well, I have every confidence that the Minister of Militia and Defence will not lose a moment to investigate in what respect he can reduce the expenditure, while at the same time pro-118}
viding for the increased expenditures that must come from time to time. With regard to the Post Office Department, the commissioners say as follows:-
Your commissioners find that this is the third of the big_departments scheduled under the Civil Service Act. As far as the commissioners can ascertain, the working of this department is conducted in a good businesslike manner, and except for the intervention of politics, and, possibly, the desire to run the department too cheaply, no fault can be found with the administraion.
I wonder if our hon. friends opposite complain of the Post Office Department because it is running affairs too cheaply. While we would regret if the Postmaster General were obliged to turn a deaf ear to certain requests made to him for improvement of postal facilities, I am sure every hon. gentleman in this House will rejoice that the Civil Service Commission state that the only fault to be found with that department is that the minister is running it too cheaply. There is no suggestion there of any wrong-doing. Now, I come to the Department of Railways and Canals:
Your commissioners do not propose to make any specific remarks about this department, although it is a great expending department and also has large revenues derived from the government railways. The present Deputy Minister of Railways, who has not been long in office, has established a new system of bookkeeping on the Intercolonial Railway, and it would seem probable that improvements will be effected generally.
I might go through all the departments referred to, and not in one instance do the commissioners reflect in the slightest degree upon the minister in charge, or upon the administration of the department. Then I come back to the sole point under discussion, and when I state that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has discharged his duty in dismissing the officials who have been found guilty of wrong-doing, when I state that by order in council the government have undertaken to dismiss every one of those men who have been proved guilty of dereliction of duty, I am satisfied" that no reasonable gentleman on either side of the House can refuse to accept that act as an answer to the charge made by the hon. gentleman who moved the resolution. Another matter I desire to refer to is of the contract entered into between the department and Halliday Bros., of the city of Quebec. It was stated by the hon. member for St. Annes that the original contract was for the use of their steamer at $125 a day, and that subsequently that sum was increased to $200 a day, and the insinuation is there made, that the late minister in charge of the department was responsible for that. But Mr. Justice Cassels in his report states:

Repeatedly during the examination of Colonel Gourdeau lie stated that he could bring evidence to corroborate his statement that the variation took place with the assent of the late minister. The witness referred to was Mr. Power, late member for Quebec. I invited Colonel Gourdeau to produce the evidence. No such evidence has been given and I have to judge of the matters on the evidence adduced before me. In a great many respects the evidence of Colonel Gourdeau was unsatisfactory and contradictory.
Not a single suggestion is made in the report of Mr. Justice Ca3sels to show that the late Minister of Marine and Fisheries was in any way responsible for increasing the amount of Halliday Brothers' contract'; but on the contrary he stated that Mr. Gour-deau's promise that he would produce evidence in that regard had not been fulfilled and he was obliged to come to the conclusion that the late minister had nothing whatever to do with it. The hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Maddin) referred to the fact that hon. gentlemen who were implicated with respect to these charges had not been haled before the court. I shall speak for a moment of the hon. the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. There is a court in this conutry, the highest court we have, the high court of public opinion. Down in the county of Rouville there is such a court, the court of the people of the county of Rouville, the county represented by the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries. In view of all the charges made against the minister in the last 12 months with respect to maladministration in his department one would imagine these hon. gentlemen would have made good and would have availed themselves of the earliest opportunity to appeal to that court and to prove there that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries was no longer worthy of their confidence and should not be returned to represent them in parliament again. It is a most extraordinary circumstance that the one minister against whom all their attacks and all their shafts were levelled for 12 months was allowed on the 26th of October to be returned by acclamation to this House. Surely if these hon. gentlemen were sincere, surely if they felt the full responsibility of the charges they made against the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and against his department, they would have taken the earliest opportunity to have prevented the minister from coming back to preside over the department which they insinuated he had so ineffectively and so dishonestly administered. If there was one constituency in the whole of this broad Dominion that they should have fought and fought to the death in the last election that was Rouville, in order to prevent that minister coming back to disgrace the high office he had held, as they would have expressed it. But the only constituency in Canada which they allowed to go by acclamation was Roqyille, *

and surely that is the best answer and the only answer that is required to the charges against the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. It is quite true that we had the pleasure of listening to a high certificate of character in respect to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries this afternoon given by the hon. member who moved this resolution (Mr. Doherty). I was not unprepared to hear that because I had felt ever since the election of the 26th of October last, that the hon. gentlemen opposite when it would be up to them to produce evidence to support their contentions would find it exceedingly difficult to carry on their campaign any longer. I was prepared to hear the hon. member for St Anne (Mr. Doherty) paying high eneoniums to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and why should I devote one instant of time more to defend the hon. minister against charges which have been thoroughly dissipated, from which he has been completely vindicated, charges which hon. gentlemen themselves testified this afternoon are absolutely without any foundation in fact. But, Sir, perhaps it is not desirable that the senses of the people of Canada should be steeped in forgetfulness with respect to the record of the Conservative party themselves when they were in power. The hon. member for South Cape Breton made an admission which was so significant that I shall refer to it. He said that whenever the Liberal party wanted a precedent for corruption they went back to the regime of the Conservative party. That statement is so absolutely true that I was rather amazed that the hon. gentleman found himself called upon to make it. I shall not go over the lurid history that filled the pages of ' Hansard ' from 1878 to 1896, but I shall cite one case to show that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries should not be held responsible for anything that his officials did, particularly when those acts were committed hundreds of miles away from his direct supervision. I shall refer to the case of the Curran bridge which was investigated here in 1894, and was one of the last cases investigated prior to the defeat of the Conservative party. A vote of $170,000 was asked by the Conservative government for the construction of the Curran bridge in Montreal. The hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. John Haggart) was then Minister of Railways and Canals. The construction of the bridge was undertaken by day's work, not by tender and contract, and it was found that instead of $170,000 being sufficient to complete that work, it cost nearly $400,000.- No pains were taken by the Minister of Railways of that day to supervise the carrying out of that contract or to ascertain for himself whether the money was honestly spent. I exonerate the ex-minister from any dereliction of duty in that regard, for notwithstanding the fact that the work was carried on only three

hours' ride from here, in Montreal, within easy rail, telephone and telegraph communication, although the minister could much more easily have an eye on the supervision of that work than the Minister of Marine and Fisheries could have upon a horde of officers scattered all over Canada, I do not say that the mere fact that money was grossly misspent is any personal reflection on the ex-Minister of Railways. When this came up in parliament it was proved beyond peradventure that this money was misspent to such a degree as had never been heard of in any committee of this House. The quantity of lumber required to be used was 2,594,000 feet, and there was charged and paid for 3,613,000 feet, or a steal of over 1,000,000 feet representing over $15,000. The stone-cutting which should haye been $16,000 was $40,000. Upon the Wellington street bridge the cost of stone-cutting by day's work, which should have been $3,000, was $16,715, and the Grand Trunk bridge work, which should have cost $3,000, cost the government $23,180. The attention of the government was called to that condition of affairs by certain references made to it in this parliament and by certain items in the Montreal press. The ex-Minister of Railways then undertook to investigate and he found every charge made in respect to the expenditure of that money was absolutely true. In the session of 1894, Sir Richard Cartwright, then a member of this House, moved a resolution censuring the government in respect to that work. The concluding paragraph of that resolution reads:
That in the opinion of this House, the Department of Railways and Canals is deserving of the severest censure for inefficiency, neglect of duty, extravagance and the general management in connection with the said works.
The defence made then by the Hon. Mr. Haggart, Minister of Railways, was just such a defence as I would expect he would make, and I believe every word of it; he said:
I never heard, until the evidence was given in the Public Accounts Committee the other day, that there were a number of men transferred from Mr. Kennedy's roll to Mr. St. Louis's pay-roll, and I may as well here show how impossible it was for me to find out the frauds which I knew were being committed there. I knew that the timber charged for wa9 in excess of what was required for the purpose of building that bridge; I knew that the labouj; charged for could not possibly be employed in its construction, and I knew that the demands mado upon the department were in excess of what was honestly used in the construction of the work. I tried every possible means to get at the bottom of the frauds, and to that end I had the detective force employed on the Intercolonial Railway sent up and put on the Montreal works; but I found it impossible to discover where the frauds were committed. I had great difficulty in obtaining the evidence of the time-keeper, Mr. Doheny, for the purpose of defending the government against an action brought by Mr. St. Louis in the Exchequer Court for a sum of money, amounting, I think, to $67,000 or $68,000. I had great difficulty in getting evidence sufficient to prove that there had been frauds on_the work.
Again he said:
The chief engineer reported the condition of affairs to me, setting forth that, so far as Mr. Douglas had been able to investigate, he believed the cost would reach no less a sum than $360,000, but that Mr. Douglas would continue his investigation. Mr. Douglas continued his investigation, and reported that he believed the cost of the bridges would exceed the amount he had already named.
Here we have the Minister of Railwaya in the Conservative government setting up as his defence that it was impossible for him to be cognizant of this wrong-doing which was perpetrated only 100 miles from the city of Ottawa; that defence prevailed, and the motion of Sir Richard Cartwright was voted down, every Conservative member voting to justify the minister. The hon. Mr. Haggart declared that the money was mis-spent without his knowledge, that he could not personally supervise the expenditure, that he was deceived and misled by his officials, and is it not fair to ask this House now to declare that the wrong-doing in the Department of Marine and Fisheries was absolutely without the cognizance of the minister and was such that it was absolutely impossible for him to detect it.
I was not in when the hon. gentleman began his remarks, but might I ask him if he is referring to the Quebec Bridge?

Here in the mother country there can be only one feeling, that of deep regret for the wrong done to the fair fame of the eldest of her daughters.

public life in Canada from the taint of corruption, the like of which we have not seen in our own country for hundreds of years.

These English newspapers perfectly describe the condition of affairs in Canada from 1891 to 1896, and there is absolute truth in the statement made by the hon. gentleman for South Cape Breton when he said that we were obliged to go to the regime of the Tory party to find precedents for corruption in this country. The hon. member for St. Anne (Mr. Doherty) gave a certificate of character to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and although the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Maddin) used much stronger language and exhibited much more temper than his colleague (Mr. Doherty) he also paid a compliment to the minister. He said that he would not now make a complaint against the administration of that hon. gentleman, but that a charge would be made at another time. I wonder if the hon. gentleman had in mind the time some years hence when this parliament will be dissolved and the right hon. the Prime Minister will age in appeal for the support of the electors. I wonder if the hon. gentleman from Cape Breton thought that when that time comes around he will revamp these charges against the Minister of Marine. Well, Sir, I tell him and I tell others that here and now are the place and time to make charges against any minister of this government and not when the election campaign is on and when they can give free scope to their unfettered imagination and irresponsible rhetoric. When the Liberals were in opposition in this country they made charges in this House, they met the accused face to face and they asked for committees to be allowed to prove these charges. That was the manly course to take, but the Conservative government then in power made sure that if an inquiry were granted the accused should be surrounded by all the technicalities the law' afforded for their protection. The resolution of the hon. member for St. Anne simply calls for an inquiry into other departments of government to see if any wrong-doing has been committed. We are bound to assume, as these gentlemen opposite have failed to make charges, that the truth is that having made all the inquiry they could they are unable to point a finger at one single act of maladministration committed by any minister of the Crown. The hon. gentleman from St. Anne gave his case away when he said a cloud of suspicion rested on the Mr. KYTE.
department. Well, there is no cloud of
suspicion in the minds of gentlemen on this side of the House, and in view of the result of the elections on the 26th of October last I venture to say there is no cloud of suspicion in the minds of the electorate of this country. And, Sir, the government having been charged by the people of Canada with the full responsibility of conducting the affairs of this country, I believe they can find themselves much better employed than in appointing roving commissions to investigate foundationless charges. As I understand it, the charge made against the government is not that certain officials of the Marine and Fisheries Department have bleen guilty of wrongdoing. One can easily understand some of the officials of so large a department as the Department of Marine and Fisheries going wrong, and it would be unreasonable to find fault with the minister or the government if the minister, on ascertaining the wrong-doing, or at the time he should have ascertained it with ordinary vigilance, had dismissed the wrong-doer and punished him, as the law provides. What we charge is, that not only the head of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, but the head of the government who knew, or ought to have known, of the wrong-doing of * these men three or four years before they were dismissed, did not take the course they should have taken. We also charge that at the present time, they are not taking the course they should take with reference to the men whose guilt has been established. and respecting what the ministers knew of the wrong-doing, they were not allowed to give evidence with regard to that. The commissioner himself gives in substance the scope of the inquiry where he says:
Thereupon the commission, dated the 6th April, 1908, appointed me commissioner ' to investigate and report upon certain statements contained in the report of the Civil Service Commission reflecting upon the integrity of the ofliciais of the Department of the Marine and Fisheries, or some of them.
Not the integrity of the government or the integrity of the ministers, but the integrity of the officials. Then he goes on to say:
Some limitation had to be given to the inquiry, and as the charges made by the report of the Civil Service Commission are mainly confined to the fiscal years 1904-5, 1905-6 and 1906-7, I limited the investigation in the meantime to those years.
So that the scope of the investigation is to inquire as to the integrity of certain officials and as to their conduct during those three years. The evidence adduced before the honourable the commissioner, covers nearly 2,200 large pages of printed matter, and the report of the commissioner, which is composed largely of quotations from the evidenc, covers 78 pages. I do not propose to detain the House to go over all the evidence contained in these 2,200 large pages of printed matter; but any hon. member who has read that evidence and the report of the commissioner must have reached these conclusions which I propose to read as the conclusions which I have reached on a fair reading of the evidence and the report:
(1)	. That the Department of Marine and Fisheries as a whole was loosely, extravagantly and dishonestly carried on.
(2)	. That both judge and counsel were anxious that all the officials should be able to prove themselves innocent, and that every opportunity to that end was given them. I have not drawn this conclusion with any intention of reflecting on either the counsel or the judge, but simply to show that every individual who was charged, or against whom there was any suspicion, was accorded the most ample opportunity to come forward and clear himself.
(3)	. That the investigation which was actually had, was fragmentary, disconnected and incomplete.
(4)	. That large numbers of officials were shown, even by such a partial inquiry, to have been dishonest.
(5)	. That the fraudulent transactions extended over at least three years, from 1904 to 1907, to which the inquiry was limited, although there was some evidence reaching into the year 1908.
(6)	. That there was an utter absence of any man, from the Prime Minister down
to the petty agent, exerting any intelligent zeal for the protection of the treasury.
(7)	. That owing to the limited scope of the commission, the responsibility for the shameful conditions exposed, was not fixed.
(8)	. That grounds are disclosed, which demand a thorough examination into the workings of the other great spending departments of the government and a completion of the partial investigation already had in the Department of Marine and Fisheries.

Minister of Marine presented to us this afternoon, as to the improvements and changes effected in his department, I may he allowed simply to recall that it is under the rule of the present minister that there was introduced a new system of book-keeping which ensures to the country, as we have seen, a large saving; that careless officers have been suspended; that a central purchase office, praised by Judge Cassels, was instituted; that a system of calling for tenders was adopted and patronage lists abolished.
The conduct of the minister on that occasion, as on many others, will have been for us of the younger generation of Canada, an object lesson in uprightness and energy.
Who is it, Mr. Speaker, who has helped the most in winning that economic victory whereby we are enabled to lead an independent life and to realize with pride that there exists a Canadian nation, an industrial and commercial nation, which has taken its place among the others by asserting what has been very aptly termed its economical independence.
Who is it, Mr. Speaker, if not the Minister of Marine, who has contributed in the greatest measure to ensuring to the business classes of this country the benefit of that great deed which has for its title the ' Franco-Canadian Treaty '.
You have read, Mr. Speaker, that statement of a writer particularly well informed as regards our country, in a book entitled ' Canada and its two nationalities '. The time is probably not far away when the development of the Dominion's resources will be on a great scale and possibly will bear comparison with that of its neighbour the United States. It is creditable to us that such a comparison should be made, and the mere fact of its being possible is in itself an argument.
Indeed the hon. Minister of Marine in providing so thoroughly for the improvement of our ports and our great river St. Lawrence -having perceived that there lies the key to our future success as a business people, and that since it reaches into the heart of the country, we are bound to deepen it to the innermost point, so as to carry the ocean as it were to the threshold of the Western country-has frightened that giant of producers, the United States, and more particularly New York.
In view of these gigantic works and useful reforms, it might have been expected
that the opposition would look beyond their ordinary range and spare their criticism to the man who had accomplished such things. Careless or dishonest officers in other departments, should there be any, knowing what treatment they may expect as a result of any wrong-doing, will take means to conceal the truth from any commission of inquiry, and thereby will prevent any such commission from getting at the facts.

Partisan newspapers and speakers, well known to hon. gentlemen on the other side, will cast aspersions on honest men, who are bound to vindicate their reputation for the sake of their family, of their province, of their country. sion, appointed in May, 1907, was composed of three business men of the highest character. Their report was full of serious and grave charges. In consequence of that report, Mr. Justice Cassels was appointed on April 6, 1908. He is a gentleman held in the highest esteem and respect wherever he is known. At great expense of labour and time, he inserted the probe a little deeper into the affairs of the Marine and Fisheries Department; but, unfortunately, the worst disclosures were not revealed until after the general elections were held. The result of that investigation by Mr. Justice Cassels was to verify the disclosures of the Civil Service Commission. Now, there has been a great deal of discussion as to what the real scope of the commission should have been. On this side of the House there is but one opinion, namely, that a free hand should have been given to Mr. Justice Cassels to inquire into the Marine and Fisheries Department, not confining him to the years from 1904 to 1907, or to any special years or any particular subject. The conception of his duties by the Hon. Mr. Cassels was very limited and circumscribed. According to his own idea, he was merely to investigate the contracts entered into during the years from 1904 to 1907, and ascertain the prices that were paid, the current market prices, and the discounts, if any. His attitude towards the officials of the department i,s thus expressed in his own. words, as found on page 1723 of the evidence:-
As far as I am concerned, I am here to protect these officials in every possible way. I do not want to see them guilty if it is possible to acquit them.
In my opinion, that was not the proper attitude in which to approach the investigation. He should have gone into it as an investigating judge to find guilty any who were guilty. At page 7 of the report, he also says:-
My desire has been to exculpate and not to incriminate.
According to the scope of his commission, I submit that Mr. Justice Cassels' inquiry should have embraced the names of the beneficiaries of the excessive prices. No one in this House imagines for a moment that the contract and supply men who received such excessive prices, kept those excessive prices for themselves. As to the use of the vessel itself.
