The failure of the minister to prosecute, although the funds of the department had been misappropriated, shows acquiescence in the criminal acts committed, and makes . him to that extent responsible. I submit that the accumulation of evidence against the minister fixes the responsibility upon him, and in order to refresh the memory of the hon. gentleman, I desire to repeat the facts in connection with the investigation which in my opinion fasten responsibility upon him. First, that goods were bought by the department without tender; patented goods were bought at excessive prices in defiance of the patent Act; men were kept in their positions and some of them like Captain Johnston promoted when they were guilty of irrgularities; that the minister was written to several times in regard to the Halliday account but paid no attention; that that account was delayed for nine months before a settlement was made by the department, and that $3,000 had to be paid to Mr. Boudreau an official of the department before it was paid.
That is not true.

I am taking the sworn evidence of Van Felson that $3 000 was paid before the account was settled, and that Mr. Boudreau told him that before that account would be settled there had to be $3,000 paid and divided between Boudreau and some one else in the department. The next thing that fixes responsibility upon the minister is the increase in the staff during October, and that the minister knowing that Captain Johnston had kept
$1,900 of the public money improperly, failed to prosecute. The question is: what is the responsibility of the minister and the cabinet. Under the principles of the British constitution there were two courses onen to the first minister, one being to ask for the resignation of the responsible head of the department, to reorganize the department and to let the blame rest where it should rest, namely, on the head of the department. The other course was for the Prime Minister to retain in the cabinet the head of that department and to shoulder the responsbility. I submit that in England the responsible head of a department which had fallen into such disgrace would not have been retained in the cabinet for 24 hours. No government in the old country would be able in defiance of public opinion to retain a responsible minister of the Crown whose department had been so discredited. It has been proven by incontrovertible evidence that the Department of Marine and Fisheries is a mass of jobbery and corruption and crime. This has been proven and reported upon by Mr. Judge Cassels, and notwithstanding, it would appear that the government is determined to defend the Minister of Marine at all hazards. Whether that be a case of choice or necessity I know not, but my own opinion is that it is a matter of necessity because the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, conscious that his department is no worse than others, is not prepared to be made the scapegoat of the administration. He has his back to the wall and he tells the others that they have to stand or fall together, and so he refuses to resign or to relieve the government from responsibility. The Minister of Marine in his defence stated that he should not be held responsible, and he gave as a reason that he was onlv continuing the system that had been inaugurated by his predecessors. All authorities on the question of ministerial responsibility fix the responsibility first on the minister himself and secondly on the cabinet as a whole if the minister remains in the cabinet and is defended. I quote from Mr. Todd's parliamentary government volume 1, page 628. 2nd edition.
As a necessary consequence of the division of the Civil Service into political and nonpolitical officers, and of the acknowledged supremacy of the members of the administration over all the subordinate employees, it is required by our parliamentary system that every branch of the public service should bo represented, either directly or indirectly, in the Houses of parliament. This duty is performed by the political heads who are themselves solely responsible for every Act of administration down to the minutest details of official routine.
In the face of such a high authority how can the Minister of Marine hold up his

officials hands and say they are clean, and that he is not responsible. Todd, page 472, volume 2, speaking of the responsibility of ministers of the Crown to parliament, says:
Notwithstanding the modern rules of parliamentary government whereby responsibility is attached to the whole administration for the acts of the several members of which the same is composed, the ancient rule that the constitution of this country always selects for responsibility the individual minister who does any particular act continues to hold good, and is directly applicable in cases of personal misconduct for which the collective administration decline to be answerable.
Speaking of the collective responsibility of the ministers Todd says. Todd, vol. ii, p. 477, 2nd edition:
The true doctrine on this subject was afterwards enunciated by the Earl of Grey in the following terms:	the essence of responsible
government is, that mutual bond of responsibility one for another, wherein a government, acting by party, go together, frame their measures in concert, and where if one member falls to the ground, the others, almost as a matter of course, fall with him.
But the application of this principle would be often partial and insufficient for the ends of justice were it not for the exception implied in Lord Derby's definition and which admits of a definite and unqualified responsibility being exclusively attached to a minister of the Crown who is proved to have done anything which renders him personally liable to the censure of parliament or to punishment by legal process.
In view of that authority, the responsibility is upon the administration for the acts of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. And what does the government propose to do? I submit that their action in superannuating two head officials, dismissing nine others, and dismissing 12 others with a string to their dismissal, is not sufficient in view of the serious charges made against the department. For the sake of the Civil Service and for the sake of the country do they purpose inaugurating any reform? I do not believe that the poor officials in the Marine Department are alone responsible for the woeful lack of moral stamina in the service. As was eloquently said by the member for Elgin (Mr. Croth-ers) it is not at the bottom but at the top we should look for the lack of moral stamina which prevails in the public service of the country. I believe, Sir, that in view of the evidence brought out by the Cassels investigation this House should extend the investigation to all the other spending departments of the government, and adopt the resolution moved by my hon. friend from St.Anne (Mr. Doherty.).

Mr. Speaker, I do not purpose in the course of the few remarks I intend making, to answer-and I say it without wishing to Mr. S. SHARPE.
be offensive-the scrap-book oration of the hon. gentleman from North Ontario (Mr. 'Sharpe), jin my humble judgment, in spite of the numerous quotations with which he has favoured us to-night, he has not succeeded in advancing a single argument to justify this House in passing a condemnation upon the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, or upon the Cabinet of which he is a member, or in voting for the resolution which has been placed before you by the hon. member for St. Anne (Mr. Doherty). I do not propose either to defend the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries. The hon. minister showed, this afternoon, in the most remarkable manner, that he is quite able to defend himself and the administration of the department of which he is the head. But my object in rising to-night is simply to place myself on record, in order to show my appreciation of the most excellent work which the hon. minister has performed for his country, and especially for the great port of this country, which I have the honour to represent in this House, since he has been entrusted with the responsibility of a minister of the Crown. Before proceeding any further, Mr. Speaker, I must congratulate most heartily the hon. member for St. Anne, on the fairness and moderation which have characterized the address which he has delivered in support of his motion. I may say that I have known that hon. gentleman for many years, and I expected that while he might feel it to be his duty to offer the resolution which he has submitted to-night, he would do it m a manner that would be consistent with the tone of our debates and the dignity of this House. Looking back to the record of this House for the last year, and remembering the discussions which took place last session, when the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries was trying to get his estimates passed, and when the hon. members opposite felt it to be part of their duty to resort to obstructive tactics, I think I am justified in believing that if the hon. member for St. Anne had had a seat in this House at that time, instead of joining in the chorus, he would have entered a vigorous protest against such conduct. However, I regret that I cannot congratulate the hon. member for St. Anne upon either the logic of his motion or the greater part of the address which he has delivered in support of it. The whole of his motion, as well as his argument in support of it, are based upon the assumption that because some wrong-doing was found to exist in some of the departments of the administration the other large departments, which he has not even named, must be subject to suspicion, and that, in order to lift the cloud of suspicion which overhangs them, this House should appoint a

commission, which might be called a fishing commission, in order to ascertain whether these suspicions are well-founded or not. This is the whole argument of the hon. gentleman, and I believe I am fair to him in stating that he has not advanced another argument to justify the position he has taken in this House upon this question.
In all fairness I must say that the hon. member for St. Anne has exonerated the hon. Minister,of Marine and Fisheries from any blame, so far as his personal honour is concerned; and in giving expression to that sentiment he is certainly reflecting the sentiment not only of all of the members on this side of the House, but also of those who had an opportunity of becoming acquainted with the minister's policy, his method of administration, and his patriotism. He is also expressing the sentiment of the whole country, which, in the last general election demonstrated their approval, not only of the administration, but most particularly of those members of the administration who have been most signally attacked by the opposition, either in the press or on the hustings.
In regard to the matter under discussion, there are two questions which have to be considered: First, a question of fact; and second, a question of law, constitutional law-a question of ministerial responsibility. As to the question of fact, everybody admits that there was in the Department of Marine and Fisheries a condition of affairs that was certainly regrettable, and that it was the duty of the government to apply the proper remedy. I cannot understand how hon. gentlemen opposite are trying to argue that the condition of affairs as disclosed by the report of Mr. Justice Cassels, was calculated to cast suspicion on the department, when that very commission was appointed as a step towards applying a remedy. I do not understand why our hon. friends opposite are insisting on so many conditions, in view of the fact that the hon. minister has accepted the conclusions of the commission and himself has applied the remedy.
As regards the question of ministerial responsibility, I am at a loss to understand the logical connection between the acts of some officials who were appointed under the late administration and the administration of the minister. The minister certainly had every right to believe that these officials were worthy of their trust, since hon. gentlemen opposite had given them, during their 18 years' administration, their fullest confidence and had never lifted a finger to remove one of them from office. I am at a loss, therefore, to see what logical connection there can be between the acts of these officials and the conduct of the head of the department. But if there were circumstances which justified the appointment of Mr. Justice Cassels as commissioner, those circumstances are entirely lacking to justify the appointment of the commission asked for by the hon. member for St. Anne (Mr. Doherty). There i3 no doubt responsibility in this matter, but what is the responsibility with which the Minister of Marine and Fisheries may be charged? It is the responsibility of having attempted to do, and having succeeded in doing, what none of his predecessors ever attempted, namely, to reform his own department. In this connection, I quite agree with my hon. friends opposite that there is responsibility to fasten upon the minister, but not responsibility of a nature calculated to reflect injuriously upon him or upon his colleagues. Some of the reforms inaugurated by the minister have been mentioned by some of the preceding speakers. The hon. minister himself, speaking in his own defence, said that during the three years of his tenure of office he had made some improvements, not only in the ordinary management of his own department, but also outside his department, in the line of bettering our system of transportation and in a general way seconding the efforts of nature and extending to the St. Lawrence route the advantages nature intended it to enjoy, and which are destined to make it the navigation route par excellence of the North American continent. But with that modesty which characterizes him, he did not tell the House that, of all the Ministers of Marine and Fisheries, he is surely the one who has done the most to improve our system of transportation by water and to put our River St. Lawrence in a condition which makes it the rival route of New York to-day, and will to-morrow make it the superior of that route in every respect. Speaking particularly as the representative of a division which forms part of the great metropolis of Canada, I consider it my duty to say that in Montreal there is but one voice in admitting that the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries has done remarkably well in putting the River St. Lawrence, and the port of Montreal in particular, upon a first-class footing. My hon. friend the minister quoted some of the resolutions passed by the board of trade and other commercial bodies of Montreal, but he did not say that to-day it is universally admitted in the commercial and financial circles of Montreal that the present government, and particularly the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries, have done more for the people of this country and the port of Montreal than was accomplished in any previous regime.
Speaking in a language with which I am not very familiar, I cannot help but feel that I am wearying the House and shall consequently not make any lengthy remarks. But referring again to what has been accomplished by this government with

regard to navigation, I shall take the liberty of quoting the report of the Hon. Mr. Justice Cassels. On page 9 of that report, Mr. Justice Cassels says:
The improvements of the navigation of the St. Lawrence and the upper lakes has been the subject of consideration by various administrations that have held office since confederation. In 1900 a more vigorous policy was adopted than has been pursued to the present time.
Well, in 1900, by the grace of God, a Liberal government was presiding over the destinies of this country, and because of that fact, a vigorous policy was adopted in order to make the River St. Lawrence and our general system of water transportation the best in America. There is another reform which has been effected by this government, and for the initiation of which we must give credit to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. Those who were in this House three years ago will remember that I had the privilege of advocating a reform which, in my opinion, was intimately, connected with the future of Montreal. I said that the time had arrived to introduce into the management of that port a new system which would give impetus to the various works undertaken in it and would place that port upon a footing it had not then reached, owing to the laxity of its former management. And I had the pleasure of seeing that a few days after the hon. minister, understanding the requirements of the situation and feeling that the time had arrived to infuse a new spirit into the management of the port, introduced a Bill whereby the old management was done away with and a new management substituted, more in harmony with the situation and the conditions in the port.
And, Mr. Speaker, I have the evidence of the commercial men, and financiers of Montreal, whether Liberal or Conservative, that no reform was ever made calculated to so greatly advance the progress of the great metropolis of Canada. And perhaps I may be permitted, in passing, to pay a deserved tribute to the new commissioners who have been appointed under the guidance of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries for the noble work they have performed. I am in a position to declare, under the responsibility that attaches to my declaration as a member of this House, that to-day the port of Montreal is in a position to compete with American ports, and especially with the port of New York. I may be charged with taking a narrow view of this question, and advocating only the interest of the city of Montreal; but, as I have said, this is not a local question or one to be treated from a selfish or narrow standpoint of local interest, but from a broadly national standpoint. And, as I have said, the interests of the port of Montreal are undoubtedly bound up with the interests of all Canada. We members must all recognize, Mr. RIVET.
whether we be from Quebec, from Toronto, Halifax, or St. John, that we must equip our national port-if I may be permitted to use the expression-in a first-class manner, if we want to compete in a successful way with the port of New York. Well, Sir, this is no new thing. Everybody has seen in the newspapers that, not long ago, the railway companies of the United States decided to reduce their rates to New York in order to enable the New York route to compete with the St. Lawrence route, because last year the grain traffic, instead of taking the route to Buffalo and New York, took the St. Lawrence route by way of Montreal. But, in spite of this reduction, we are in a position to compete successfully with the port of New York, and I believe that if Montreal has been placed on such a footing, it is due largely, if not wholly, to the wise policy, the noble efforts and the far-sighted administration of this government under the initiative of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
The fact has been referred to in this House that, owing to the improvements made, the rates of insurance have been reduced by a total of about $200,000. Everybody understands that, if the owners of steamers are able to save so much simply on the rates of insurance, they are immediately put in an advantageous position as compared with their rivals of other countries. Everybody knows that to-day great improvements have been made in the channel between Quebec and Montreal. Some people may say: 'You speak always from the standpoint of Montreal.' I do not wish to be charged with a selfish spirit. .If I were not convinced, as I am, that the interests of Montreal are the interests of the whole country, I -would not stand up in this House and advocate discrimination even in favour of my own city.
In view of the attacks which have been heaped upon the methods of administration of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, I thought it was my duty, as I think it the duty of every member, whether he comes from the province of Quebec or not, to stand up in this House and-to use the expression of the hon. member for Berthier (Mr. Ecrement), to say a little on his behalf'. I believe that everybody who knows the minister will agree with me when I acquit him of any wrong-doing or even bad intention. At the last election, as some of the speakers have said, a compact was entered into between the administration and the electors of this country. They had gone before the people and had told them that, in view of the attacks and criticisms levelled against the Department of Marine and Fisheries, the government had appointed a commission which would investigate and probe to the bottom every charge made against the department, and, should the report of His Lordship Judge Cassels

pass condemnation upon any official in the government that official would be dealt with. The electors listened to that proposal and extended their confidence and support to the present administration. And now, when the first opportunity presents itself to go into the recommendations of the commissions, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries does his duty, and redeems his pledge to the people by dismissing these officials-very much against his feelings. As he said this afternoon he has been in receipt of pathetic appeals from mothers and wives. But in the conscientious discharge of his duties towards the administration and the country, he dismissed all who were found guilty of wrong-doing. We have fulfilled our contract with the people. And what have hon. gentlemen opposite to say? I say that they stand up there one after another, trying to open a case which, to my mind, is closed forever. They are not sincere, because, when the government appointed Mr. Justice Cassels, the opposition as well as the government supporters felt that the appointment was a worthy one, and that the country could trust Mr. Justice Cassels' findings. But now, because those findings do not go as far as their wishes-the wish being father to the thought-they place themselves in the position of a judge and try to render a verdict which the judge has not rendered, in order to satisfy themselves and their sympathizers that the government is not worthy the confidence of the country. Now this is the position, and it is a position which justifies the representatives of the electorate in placing their confidence in the members of the administration, and especially in the hon. the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
It was said by the last speaker (Mr. Samuel Sharpe) that now, surely, the minister ought to resign. Why, Mr. Speaker? Because, during the three years of his administration he has performed his duty, a thing which the head of that department during the Conservative regime had never done. The hon. minister must resign, because he enjoys the fullest confidence of the country, and particularly of his native province. He must resign, because, in the last election, the opposition, though well organized, could not find 25 men to place a candidate in the field against him. The minister must resign, because he has proved to be a worthy leader of his own province. The minister must resign, because to-day there is only one voice to testify to his sterling qualities, to his noble character, to his honest purpose, to his patriotism, to all those qualities which make a man worthy to represent his constituents in the councils of the nation. The minister must resign, because to-day we are just as proud of him as we were yesterday, and just as
willing to follow him and to serve our country under his direction. Sir, in conclusion let me say that I have read carefully the motion which has been placed in your hands, I have listened attentively to the addresses which have been delivered in support of that motion, and sitting as a member of the popular jury, I must come to the conclusion that no argument ha3 been adduced which would justify me in giving a verdict in favour of the motion now before the Chair.

One of the last remarks made by the hon. member for Hochelaga (Mr. Rivet), who has just taken his seat, was to the effect that he had carefully read the motion which is before the House. Of all the remarks uttered by that gentleman that was the most surprising to me, because, throughout the entire course of an address lasting I believe over an hour, it was the only remark that bore any possible relation to the words of the motion at all. I regret that, owing to the lateness of the hour, and owing to the fact that to answer the hon. gentleman would require me to disregard utterly the motion itself, it will be impossible for me to give much attention to his address. As to the gentleman who preceded him, the hon. member for Berthier (Mr. Ee-rement), who spoke in French, I regret, with my hon. friend from NoTth Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) that I was unable to understand his address. I regret it all the more because, though not able to understand it, I was able to appreciate the music of his voice and accent, and the apparent eloquence of his language.
The Minister of Marine and Fisheries has exhibited some remarkable qualities during the present session. I must congratulate him on the marvellous facility of intellect and the bewildering dexterity of mind that enable him to come to almost any conclusion that may be congenital to him, or satisfactory to his conscience, utterly irrespective of the facts. On April 30, almost a year ago, when his department, in conjunction with other departments, stood charged before the country with the most serious delinquencies, when he himself, as part of the department, stood charged with a lack of conscience, when his department stood charged with being utterly wanting in a directing head, as far as the commissioners could see, the minister saw fit to come before the House and tell of the hard work he had done in his department, to recount the undertakings he had carried out in the St. Lawrence river, and up in the neighbourhood of Port Arthur. No doubt he conceived that that was an answer to the charge of the Royal Commission. And when the hon. member for St. Anne (Mr. Doherty) saw fit to state that the resolution as it stands does not call in question, and does not make a question in this debate,

of the character and integrity of the minister himself, the minister saw fit at once to come to the conclusion that the member for St. Anne, speaking for this side of the House, had acknowledged the integrity of the character of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries as head of that department. Surely that was a delightful contortion of the mind, that was a beautiful piece of reasoning. The Minister of Marine has also come to another conclusion very satisfactory to his conscience. He comes before this parliament, and before we were in session more than a week, he assured this House that he had received a certificate of character, not only from the hon. member for St. Anne, but front this commission. He assured this House, and it is now on record, that he came out with his skirts clear from the report of Mr. Justice Cassels. Now it is indeed a beautiful piece of reasoning for the minister to come to the conclusion that his skirts are clear by an investigation through a commission which was forbidden above all things to investigate anything about him at all. The hon. member for Richmond also says that it can no longer be said that there is any charge against the minister, or any suspicion that can be levelled against him, because, he says, the minister is cleared by the report of Mr. Justice Cassels. But the hon. member for Richmond made that statement in face of the assurance of the Minister of Agriculture, in face of the assurance of the Attorney General of this country, in face of the assurance of the Minister of Marine himself, and of the Prime Minister himself, that Mr. Justice Cassels was forbidden to investigate any of the conduct of the minister of that department, but was restricted in his investigation to the underlings. Surely, it ill becomes a minister to look for a certificate of character to a commission that was forbidden to investigate anything that might throw any light on his own transactions in the department, or upon his own connection with the delinquencies that existed. We have heard about drowning men clutching at straws, but the anxiety of the Minister of Marine and his followers to obtain a certificate of character for their chief certainly bears a very strong resemblance to that picture. The minister in his defence practically repeats the speech he delivered in this House on April 30, 1908. He goes back and tries to show that the system which is now so much abused by this government was in vogue under Conservative administration. That argument has been very frequently combatted in this House and I do not think it can be combatted too strongly. It does seem to me that the country, and I think most members of this House, are tired of it. Surely the Minister of Marine, surely members on the other side of the House do not pretend to say that a Mr. MEIGHEN.
system that fits one time will fit all times. Surely they do not pretend to say that the successors of the Conservative party for all time to come are to be bound within whatever limits the Conservative party, 20 years ago or 30 years ago saw fit to be bound; surely they would not say that their successors in office for years to come, that their political successors shall have a circle drawn around them and be confined within the narrow limits by virtue of the present administration; surely they will allow some scope for the evolution of political morality and for improvements that will take place. It does not seem to me that it is a sufficient answer to this House and the country that the use of a patronage list in 1886 is a justification for its use years afterwards; surely they ought to make some allowance for the progress of time, surely they must admit that the times have out-grown that system. Supposing they do not admit that, it is not so much the system that is attacked, it is not so much the system that brings disgrace on this government and discredit on its members, as it is the abuse of the system. The abuse of the system seems to have taken root within the last few years. The abuse of this system has not been traced back by Mr. Justice Cassels nor indeed by the previous commission beyond the days of this government. Surely, therefore, they cannot hide behind the fact that the system existed to shield themselves from the consequences of their abuse of that system.
The Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) very rightly suggests that he should not be held responsible for the sins of his predecessors. Personally it would be unjust to hold him responsible. But the Minister of Marine, in common with other members of this government who were members of the government when the minister's predecessor, Mr. Prefontaine, held that portfolio, was responsible for the discrepancies of the Marine Department at that time. I need not take the statements of Conservatives in support of that doctrine of ministerial responsibility, but shall refer to the speeches delivered by prominent Liberals in 1891 when the late Hon. Sir Hector Lan-gevin was charged in this parliament with misconduct in his own department. They will find that one of the strongest constitutional lawyers in this conutry, the late Hon. David Mills, speaking on behalf of the opposition of that day, was very emphatic upon this point. Before quoting his words, let me briefly state the circumstances: The late Hon. Sir Hector Langevin was charged with serious misconduct in connection with the Department of Public Works. Specific charges were made against him. The matter was submitted to a special committee of this House. Two reports were presented to this House, a minority report and a majority report. The majority report specifically

and unequivocally acquitted Sir Hector Langevin from anything in the nature of active participation or any connection with the irregularitites found to exist in the department. The minority report also went so far as to find that they had not evidence to connect Sir Hector with any improper transactions. The two reports coincided in that particular, but the minority report went on-and I draw the attention of the Minister of Marine to this particularly, because they are the words of his colleague in this House, the late Hon. David Mills, and the Hon. Sir Louis Davies of the Supreme Court. At page lxxxii of the Journals of the House of Commons of Canada, A. 1891, appendix No. 1, they say :
Except the desire to please and obey the minister at the head of the department, we cannot discover any motives which would induce these engineers to assist in defrauding the public in order to put money in the pockets of Larkin, Connolly & Co.
Therefore, the ground that these men considered sufficient to connect the head of the department with the frauds perpetrated by those beneath him was that they could conceive of no other motive except that they wished to please and obey the minister at the head of the department. If that ground was good then it is good today, and if it is good now it distinctly implicates the head of the department and puts him on his defence. If the same circumstances exist now as existed then they should lead to the same conclusion.
Speaking in the light of those findings of both the majority and minority reports of those days, Mr. M. C. Cameron, then member for Huron, speaking in the House of Commons of Canada, used the following words at page 5824 of the ' Hansard ':
A member of parliament, a former political friend and supporter of hon. gentlemen opposite, has, for three hours arraigned the policy and the conduct of the hon. gentlemen opposite with respect to their administration of public works, and yet upon the ministerial benches, behind them and on each side of them, there is^ not a man who has courage enough to rise in his seat and defend the position of the government. Hon. gentlemen will remember that this is not an assault solely upon the late member for Quebec West or an assault solely upon the late Minister of Public Works. It is an assault upon every hon. gentlemen who was the colleague of the Minister of Public Works while he was a member of the present administration. They supported and sustained him, and if they know anything about parliamentary, constitutional rule, they must know perfectly well that each one of them is just as responsible as the late Minister of Public Works. I am astounded at the Minister of Justice, and the Minister of War, and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and the Minister of Finance, and above all the Secretary of State, should remain silent in their seats. Are they going to plead guilty to the charges levelled against them?
That is to say, Mr. M. C. Cameron, who was at that time put up by the right hon. gentleman who now leads the government to argue the constitutional aspect of this case as it affected the individual responsibility of the other ministers of the Crown, was made to say and did say that they all shared the responsibility for the guilt even of officials of the department on the ground only as stated in the minority report that there was a reasonable inference that these acts were done either in obedience to their wishes or their orders. As the hour is late I beg to move that the debate be adjourned.

Motion agreed to, and debate adjourned.
